items.title: Counting Boolean Functions
items.statement:
There are exactly
\[
2^{2^n}
\]
Boolean functions \(\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > There are exactly
   > \[
   > 2^{2^n}
   > \]
   > Boolean functions \(\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\).

items.title: Unique Syntax Tree for Propositional Formulas
items.statement: Every propositional well-formed formula has a unique parse tree.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every propositional well-formed formula has a unique parse tree.

items.title: Proper Subformula Depth
items.statement:
If \(\psi\) is a proper subformula of \(\varphi\), then
\[
\operatorname{depth}(\psi)<\operatorname{depth}(\varphi).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(\psi\) is a proper subformula of \(\varphi\), then
   > \[
   > \operatorname{depth}(\psi)<\operatorname{depth}(\varphi).
   > \]

items.title: Finiteness of Subformulas
items.statement: For every \(\varphi\in\WFF\), the set \(\operatorname{Sub}(\varphi)\) is finite.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every \(\varphi\in\WFF\), the set \(\operatorname{Sub}(\varphi)\) is finite.

items.title: Symmetry of Equality
items.statement: From $t_1 = t_2$, one may infer $t_2 = t_1$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > From $t_1 = t_2$, one may infer $t_2 = t_1$.

items.title: Transitivity of Equality
items.statement: From $t_1 = t_2$ and $t_2 = t_3$, one may infer $t_1 = t_3$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > From $t_1 = t_2$ and $t_2 = t_3$, one may infer $t_1 = t_3$.

items.title: Term Substitution under Equality
items.statement:
If $t_1 = t_2$, then for any function symbol $f$,
$f(\dots,t_1,\dots) = f(\dots,t_2,\dots)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $t_1 = t_2$, then for any function symbol $f$,
   > $f(\dots,t_1,\dots) = f(\dots,t_2,\dots)$.

items.title: Predicate Substitution under Equality
items.statement:
If $t_1 = t_2$ and $P$ is an $n$-ary predicate symbol, then
$P(\dots,t_1,\dots) \;\Leftrightarrow\; P(\dots,t_2,\dots)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $t_1 = t_2$ and $P$ is an $n$-ary predicate symbol, then
   > $P(\dots,t_1,\dots) \;\Leftrightarrow\; P(\dots,t_2,\dots)$.

items.title: Soundness of First-Order Logic
items.statement:
The standard inference rules for first-order logic (UI, UG, EI, EG, and the
propositional rules) are sound: they preserve truth in all structures.

If $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$, then $\Gamma \models \varphi$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The standard inference rules for first-order logic (UI, UG, EI, EG, and the
   > propositional rules) are sound: they preserve truth in all structures.
   >
   > If $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$, then $\Gamma \models \varphi$.

items.title: Quantifier Negation Laws
items.statement:
For every formula \(\varphi\),
\[
\neg\forall x\,\varphi \equiv \exists x\,\neg\varphi,
\qquad
\neg\exists x\,\varphi \equiv \forall x\,\neg\varphi.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every formula \(\varphi\),
   > \[
   > \neg\forall x\,\varphi \equiv \exists x\,\neg\varphi,
   > \qquad
   > \neg\exists x\,\varphi \equiv \forall x\,\neg\varphi.
   > \]

items.title: Negation of Bounded Quantifiers
items.statement:
Let \(A\) be a set and let \(\varphi\) be a formula. Then
\[
\neg(\forall x\in A\,\varphi)\equiv \exists x\in A\,\neg\varphi,
\qquad
\neg(\exists x\in A\,\varphi)\equiv \forall x\in A\,\neg\varphi.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(A\) be a set and let \(\varphi\) be a formula. Then
   > \[
   > \neg(\forall x\in A\,\varphi)\equiv \exists x\in A\,\neg\varphi,
   > \qquad
   > \neg(\exists x\in A\,\varphi)\equiv \forall x\in A\,\neg\varphi.
   > \]

items.title: Universal Implies Existential
items.statement:
Over nonempty domains,
\[
\forall x\,\varphi(x)\models \exists x\,\varphi(x).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Over nonempty domains,
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\varphi(x)\models \exists x\,\varphi(x).
   > \]

items.title: Existential Does Not Imply Universal
items.statement:
In general,
\[
\exists x\,\varphi(x)\not\models \forall x\,\varphi(x).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In general,
   > \[
   > \exists x\,\varphi(x)\not\models \forall x\,\varphi(x).
   > \]

items.title: Uniform Witness Implies Dependent Witness
items.statement:
For every formula \(\varphi(x,y)\),
\[
\exists y\,\forall x\,\varphi(x,y)
\models
\forall x\,\exists y\,\varphi(x,y).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every formula \(\varphi(x,y)\),
   > \[
   > \exists y\,\forall x\,\varphi(x,y)
   > \models
   > \forall x\,\exists y\,\varphi(x,y).
   > \]

items.title: Dependent Witness Need Not Be Uniform
items.statement:
In general,
\[
\forall x\,\exists y\,\varphi(x,y)
\not\models
\exists y\,\forall x\,\varphi(x,y).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In general,
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\exists y\,\varphi(x,y)
   > \not\models
   > \exists y\,\forall x\,\varphi(x,y).
   > \]

items.title: Valid Quantifier Distribution
items.statement:
For all formulas \(\varphi,\psi\),
\[
\forall x\,(\varphi\land\psi)
\equiv
(\forall x\,\varphi)\land(\forall x\,\psi),
\]
\[
\exists x\,(\varphi\lor\psi)
\equiv
(\exists x\,\varphi)\lor(\exists x\,\psi).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all formulas \(\varphi,\psi\),
   > \[
   > \forall x\,(\varphi\land\psi)
   > \equiv
   > (\forall x\,\varphi)\land(\forall x\,\psi),
   > \]
   > \[
   > \exists x\,(\varphi\lor\psi)
   > \equiv
   > (\exists x\,\varphi)\lor(\exists x\,\psi).
   > \]

items.title: Renaming Bound Variables
items.statement:
If \(y\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) and no capture is introduced, then
\[
\forall x\,\varphi\equiv\forall y\,\varphi[y/x],
\qquad
\exists x\,\varphi\equiv\exists y\,\varphi[y/x].
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(y\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) and no capture is introduced, then
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\varphi\equiv\forall y\,\varphi[y/x],
   > \qquad
   > \exists x\,\varphi\equiv\exists y\,\varphi[y/x].
   > \]

items.title: Existence of Prenex Normal Form
items.statement:
Every first-order formula is logically equivalent to some formula in prenex
normal form.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every first-order formula is logically equivalent to some formula in prenex
   > normal form.

items.title: Double Negation and Quantifiers
items.statement:
For every formula \(\varphi\),
\[
\neg\neg\forall x\,\varphi \equiv \forall x\,\varphi,
\qquad
\neg\neg\exists x\,\varphi \equiv \exists x\,\varphi.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every formula \(\varphi\),
   > \[
   > \neg\neg\forall x\,\varphi \equiv \forall x\,\varphi,
   > \qquad
   > \neg\neg\exists x\,\varphi \equiv \exists x\,\varphi.
   > \]

items.title: Same-Type Quantifier Commutation
items.statement:
Quantifiers of the same type commute:
\[
\forall x\,\forall y\,\varphi \equiv \forall y\,\forall x\,\varphi,
\qquad
\exists x\,\exists y\,\varphi \equiv \exists y\,\exists x\,\varphi.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Quantifiers of the same type commute:
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\forall y\,\varphi \equiv \forall y\,\forall x\,\varphi,
   > \qquad
   > \exists x\,\exists y\,\varphi \equiv \exists y\,\exists x\,\varphi.
   > \]

items.title: Mixed Quantifiers Do Not Commute
items.statement:
In general,
\[
\forall x\,\exists y\,\varphi
\not\equiv
\exists y\,\forall x\,\varphi.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In general,
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\exists y\,\varphi
   > \not\equiv
   > \exists y\,\forall x\,\varphi.
   > \]

items.title: Invalid Quantifier Distribution
items.statement:
In general,
\[
\forall x\,(\varphi\lor\psi)
\not\equiv
(\forall x\,\varphi)\lor(\forall x\,\psi),
\]
\[
\exists x\,(\varphi\land\psi)
\not\equiv
(\exists x\,\varphi)\land(\exists x\,\psi).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In general,
   > \[
   > \forall x\,(\varphi\lor\psi)
   > \not\equiv
   > (\forall x\,\varphi)\lor(\forall x\,\psi),
   > \]
   > \[
   > \exists x\,(\varphi\land\psi)
   > \not\equiv
   > (\exists x\,\varphi)\land(\exists x\,\psi).
   > \]

items.title: Vacuous Quantification
items.statement:
If \(x\) does not occur free in \(\varphi\), then
\[
\forall x\,\varphi\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\exists x\,\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(x\) does not occur free in \(\varphi\), then
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\varphi\equiv\varphi,
   > \qquad
   > \exists x\,\varphi\equiv\varphi.
   > \]

items.title: Substitution Lemma for Terms
items.statement:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be a structure, let \(s\) be a variable assignment, let
\(x\) be a variable, and let \(t\) and \(u\) be terms. Then
\[
\llbracket t[u/x]\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}
=
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,\,
s[x\mapsto\llbracket u\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}]}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(\mathcal M\) be a structure, let \(s\) be a variable assignment, let
   > \(x\) be a variable, and let \(t\) and \(u\) be terms. Then
   > \[
   > \llbracket t[u/x]\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}
   > =
   > \llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,\,
   > s[x\mapsto\llbracket u\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}]}.
   > \]

items.title: Substitution Lemma for Formulas
items.statement:
Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and let \(u\) be a term free for \(x\) in
\(\varphi\). For every structure \(\mathcal M\) and assignment \(s\),
\[
\mathcal M,s\models\varphi[u/x]
\Longleftrightarrow
\mathcal M,s[x\mapsto\llbracket u\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}]\models\varphi.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and let \(u\) be a term free for \(x\) in
   > \(\varphi\). For every structure \(\mathcal M\) and assignment \(s\),
   > \[
   > \mathcal M,s\models\varphi[u/x]
   > \Longleftrightarrow
   > \mathcal M,s[x\mapsto\llbracket u\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}]\models\varphi.
   > \]

items.title: Universal Translation Pattern
items.statement:
In a broad domain, an English statement of the form ``All \(A\) are \(B\)''
is translated by
\[
\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x)).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a broad domain, an English statement of the form ``All \(A\) are \(B\)''
   > is translated by
   > \[
   > \forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x)).
   > \]

items.title: Existential Translation Pattern
items.statement:
In a broad domain, an English statement of the form ``Some \(A\) are \(B\)''
is translated by
\[
\exists x\,(A(x)\land B(x)).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a broad domain, an English statement of the form ``Some \(A\) are \(B\)''
   > is translated by
   > \[
   > \exists x\,(A(x)\land B(x)).
   > \]

items.title: Conditional Translation Pattern
items.statement:
An English statement of the form ``If \(A\), then \(B\)'' is translated by
\[
A\to B,
\]
with quantifiers placed according to the variables occurring in \(A\) and \(B\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > An English statement of the form ``If \(A\), then \(B\)'' is translated by
   > \[
   > A\to B,
   > \]
   > with quantifiers placed according to the variables occurring in \(A\) and \(B\).

items.title: Negation Translation Pattern
items.statement:
The negation of a translated quantified statement is obtained by negating the
whole formula and then pushing the negation inward using the quantifier
negation laws.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The negation of a translated quantified statement is obtained by negating the
   > whole formula and then pushing the negation inward using the quantifier
   > negation laws.

items.title: A-O Contradiction
items.statement:
The \(A\)-form \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x))\) and the \(O\)-form
\(\exists x\,(A(x)\land \neg B(x))\) are contradictory: exactly one of them is
true.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The \(A\)-form \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x))\) and the \(O\)-form
   > \(\exists x\,(A(x)\land \neg B(x))\) are contradictory: exactly one of them is
   > true.

items.title: E-I Contradiction
items.statement:
The \(E\)-form \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to \neg B(x))\) and the \(I\)-form
\(\exists x\,(A(x)\land B(x))\) are contradictory: exactly one of them is true.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The \(E\)-form \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to \neg B(x))\) and the \(I\)-form
   > \(\exists x\,(A(x)\land B(x))\) are contradictory: exactly one of them is true.

items.title: Contrariety Requires Existential Import
items.statement: If \(\exists x\,A(x)\), then the \(A\)-form and \(E\)-form cannot both be true.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(\exists x\,A(x)\), then the \(A\)-form and \(E\)-form cannot both be true.

items.title: FIP--Cover Duality
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a set, $A \subseteq X$, and $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}$ a
family of subsets of $X$. Let $F_\alpha = U_\alpha^c = X \setminus U_\alpha$.
Then:
\[
\{U_\alpha\} \text{ covers } A
\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\{F_\alpha \cap A\}_{\alpha \in I} \text{ does \emph{not} have the FIP}.
\]
More precisely: the family $\{U_\alpha\}$ does \emph{not} cover $A$ if and
only if the family of closed complements $\{F_\alpha\}$ has the FIP relative
to $A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $X$ be a set, $A \subseteq X$, and $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}$ a
   > family of subsets of $X$. Let $F_\alpha = U_\alpha^c = X \setminus U_\alpha$.
   > Then:
   > \[
   > \{U_\alpha\} \text{ covers } A
   > \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
   > \{F_\alpha \cap A\}_{\alpha \in I} \text{ does \emph{not} have the FIP}.
   > \]
   > More precisely: the family $\{U_\alpha\}$ does \emph{not} cover $A$ if and
   > only if the family of closed complements $\{F_\alpha\}$ has the FIP relative
   > to $A$.

items.title: De Morgan's Laws for Indexed Families
items.statement:
Let $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an indexed family of subsets of a universe $U$.
Then
\[
U\setminus\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i
=
\bigcap_{i\in I}(U\setminus A_i).
\]
If $I\neq\varnothing$, then
\[
U\setminus\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i
=
\bigcup_{i\in I}(U\setminus A_i).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an indexed family of subsets of a universe $U$.
   > Then
   > \[
   > U\setminus\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i
   > =
   > \bigcap_{i\in I}(U\setminus A_i).
   > \]
   > If $I\neq\varnothing$, then
   > \[
   > U\setminus\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i
   > =
   > \bigcup_{i\in I}(U\setminus A_i).
   > \]

items.title: Commutativity of Union and Intersection
items.statement:
Let $A,B$ be sets. Then
\[
A \cup B = B \cup A
\quad\text{and}\quad
A \cap B = B \cap A.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B$ be sets. Then
   > \[
   > A \cup B = B \cup A
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > A \cap B = B \cap A.
   > \]

items.title: Associativity of Union and Intersection
items.statement:
Let $A,B,C$ be sets. Then
\[
(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B,C$ be sets. Then
   > \[
   > (A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > (A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C).
   > \]

items.title: Distributive Laws
items.statement:
Let $A,B,C$ be sets. Then
\[
A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C),
\]
\[
A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B,C$ be sets. Then
   > \[
   > A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C),
   > \]
   > \[
   > A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C).
   > \]

items.title: Identity and Absorption Laws
items.statement:
Let $A,B$ be sets and $U$ a universe with $A \subseteq U$. Then
\[
A \cup \varnothing = A,
\qquad
A \cap U = A,
\]
\[
A \cup (A \cap B) = A,
\qquad
A \cap (A \cup B) = A.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B$ be sets and $U$ a universe with $A \subseteq U$. Then
   > \[
   > A \cup \varnothing = A,
   > \qquad
   > A \cap U = A,
   > \]
   > \[
   > A \cup (A \cap B) = A,
   > \qquad
   > A \cap (A \cup B) = A.
   > \]

items.title: Involution of Complement
items.statement:
For any $A \subseteq U$,
\[
(A^c)^c = A.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any $A \subseteq U$,
   > \[
   > (A^c)^c = A.
   > \]

items.title: De Morgan's Laws
items.statement:
Let $U$ be a universe and $A,B \subseteq U$. Then
\[
(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c
\quad\text{and}\quad
(A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $U$ be a universe and $A,B \subseteq U$. Then
   > \[
   > (A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > (A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c.
   > \]

items.title: Principle of Set Duality
items.statement:
Any identity involving $\cup$, $\cap$, $\varnothing$, and $U$ that holds for
all subsets of a universe remains valid when each operation and constant is
replaced by its dual.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Any identity involving $\cup$, $\cap$, $\varnothing$, and $U$ that holds for
   > all subsets of a universe remains valid when each operation and constant is
   > replaced by its dual.

items.title: Representative Independence Lemma
items.statement:
Let $R$ be an equivalence relation on $A$. For any $a,b \in A$,
\[
[a] = [b]
\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
(a,b) \in R.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $R$ be an equivalence relation on $A$. For any $a,b \in A$,
   > \[
   > [a] = [b]
   > \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
   > (a,b) \in R.
   > \]

items.title: Equivalence Relations and Partitions
items.statement:
Let $A$ be a set.
- [label=(\roman*)]
- If $R$ is an equivalence relation on $A$, then $A/R$ is a partition of $A$.
- If $\mathcal{P}$ is a partition of $A$, then the relation
$R_{\mathcal{P}}$ defined by
\[
(a,b) \in R_{\mathcal{P}} \;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\exists P \in \mathcal{P} \text{ with } a \in P \text{ and } b \in P
\]
is an equivalence relation on $A$.
- These constructions are inverse: $R_{A/R} = R$ and $A/R_{\mathcal{P}} = \mathcal{P}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A$ be a set.
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - If $R$ is an equivalence relation on $A$, then $A/R$ is a partition of $A$.
   > - If $\mathcal{P}$ is a partition of $A$, then the relation
   > $R_{\mathcal{P}}$ defined by
   > \[
   > (a,b) \in R_{\mathcal{P}} \;\Longleftrightarrow\;
   > \exists P \in \mathcal{P} \text{ with } a \in P \text{ and } b \in P
   > \]
   > is an equivalence relation on $A$.
   > - These constructions are inverse: $R_{A/R} = R$ and $A/R_{\mathcal{P}} = \mathcal{P}$.

items.title: Universal Property of the Quotient Map
items.statement:
Let $R$ be an equivalence relation on $A$, let $\pi : A \to A/R$ be the
canonical surjection, and let $f : A \to B$ be any function. Then $f$ is
\emph{constant on equivalence classes} --- meaning $(a,b) \in R$ implies
$f(a) = f(b)$ --- if and only if there exists a unique function
$\bar{f} : A/R \to B$ such that
\[
f = \bar{f} \circ \pi.
\]
When it exists, $\bar{f}$ is defined by $\bar{f}([a]) = f(a)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $R$ be an equivalence relation on $A$, let $\pi : A \to A/R$ be the
   > canonical surjection, and let $f : A \to B$ be any function. Then $f$ is
   > \emph{constant on equivalence classes} --- meaning $(a,b) \in R$ implies
   > $f(a) = f(b)$ --- if and only if there exists a unique function
   > $\bar{f} : A/R \to B$ such that
   > \[
   > f = \bar{f} \circ \pi.
   > \]
   > When it exists, $\bar{f}$ is defined by $\bar{f}([a]) = f(a)$.

items.title: Uniqueness of Ordered Pairs
items.statement:
For any sets $a,b,c,d$,
\[
(a,b) = (c,d)
\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
(a = c \land b = d).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any sets $a,b,c,d$,
   > \[
   > (a,b) = (c,d)
   > \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
   > (a = c \land b = d).
   > \]

items.title: Associativity of Relation Composition
items.statement:
Let $R\subseteq A\times B$, $S\subseteq B\times C$, and
$T\subseteq C\times D$. Then
\[
T\circ(S\circ R)=(T\circ S)\circ R.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $R\subseteq A\times B$, $S\subseteq B\times C$, and
   > $T\subseteq C\times D$. Then
   > \[
   > T\circ(S\circ R)=(T\circ S)\circ R.
   > \]

items.title: Identity Laws for Relation Composition
items.statement:
Let $R\subseteq A\times B$. Then
\[
R\circ\Delta_A=R
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Delta_B\circ R=R.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $R\subseteq A\times B$. Then
   > \[
   > R\circ\Delta_A=R
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > \Delta_B\circ R=R.
   > \]

items.title: Converse Laws for Relation Operations
items.statement:
Let $R,S\subseteq A\times B$, let $T\subseteq B\times C$, and take complements
relative to the indicated Cartesian products. Then
\[
(R^{-1})^{-1}=R,\qquad
(T\circ R)^{-1}=R^{-1}\circ T^{-1},
\]
\[
(R\cup S)^{-1}=R^{-1}\cup S^{-1},\qquad
(R\cap S)^{-1}=R^{-1}\cap S^{-1},
\]
\[
(R\setminus S)^{-1}=R^{-1}\setminus S^{-1},\qquad
((A\times B)\setminus R)^{-1}=(B\times A)\setminus R^{-1}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $R,S\subseteq A\times B$, let $T\subseteq B\times C$, and take complements
   > relative to the indicated Cartesian products. Then
   > \[
   > (R^{-1})^{-1}=R,\qquad
   > (T\circ R)^{-1}=R^{-1}\circ T^{-1},
   > \]
   > \[
   > (R\cup S)^{-1}=R^{-1}\cup S^{-1},\qquad
   > (R\cap S)^{-1}=R^{-1}\cap S^{-1},
   > \]
   > \[
   > (R\setminus S)^{-1}=R^{-1}\setminus S^{-1},\qquad
   > ((A\times B)\setminus R)^{-1}=(B\times A)\setminus R^{-1}.
   > \]

items.title: Relation Composition and Boolean Operations
items.statement:
Let $P,Q\subseteq A\times B$, $R\subseteq B\times C$, and
$S,T\subseteq B\times C$. Then
\[
R\circ(P\cup Q)=(R\circ P)\cup(R\circ Q),
\qquad
(S\cup T)\circ P=(S\circ P)\cup(T\circ P).
\]
Also,
\[
R\circ(P\cap Q)\subseteq(R\circ P)\cap(R\circ Q),
\qquad
(S\cap T)\circ P\subseteq(S\circ P)\cap(T\circ P).
\]
The analogous formulas for difference and complement hold only as inclusions
or under extra hypotheses; they are not general distributive laws.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $P,Q\subseteq A\times B$, $R\subseteq B\times C$, and
   > $S,T\subseteq B\times C$. Then
   > \[
   > R\circ(P\cup Q)=(R\circ P)\cup(R\circ Q),
   > \qquad
   > (S\cup T)\circ P=(S\circ P)\cup(T\circ P).
   > \]
   > Also,
   > \[
   > R\circ(P\cap Q)\subseteq(R\circ P)\cap(R\circ Q),
   > \qquad
   > (S\cap T)\circ P\subseteq(S\circ P)\cap(T\circ P).
   > \]
   > The analogous formulas for difference and complement hold only as inclusions
   > or under extra hypotheses; they are not general distributive laws.

items.title: Associativity of Composition
items.statement:
For $f : A \to B$, $g : B \to C$, $h : C \to D$:
\[
h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For $f : A \to B$, $g : B \to C$, $h : C \to D$:
   > \[
   > h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f.
   > \]

items.title: Identity and Composition
items.statement:
For any $f : A \to B$:
\[
f \circ \id_A = f
\quad\text{and}\quad
\id_B \circ f = f.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any $f : A \to B$:
   > \[
   > f \circ \id_A = f
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > \id_B \circ f = f.
   > \]

items.title: Injectivity and Surjectivity Under Composition
items.statement:
Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$.
- [label=(\roman*)]
- If $f$ and $g$ are injective, then $g \circ f$ is injective.
- If $f$ and $g$ are surjective, then $g \circ f$ is surjective.
- If $g \circ f$ is injective, then $f$ is injective.
- If $g \circ f$ is surjective, then $g$ is surjective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$.
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - If $f$ and $g$ are injective, then $g \circ f$ is injective.
   > - If $f$ and $g$ are surjective, then $g \circ f$ is surjective.
   > - If $g \circ f$ is injective, then $f$ is injective.
   > - If $g \circ f$ is surjective, then $g$ is surjective.

items.title: Characterization of Inverse Functions
items.statement:
Let $f : A \to B$ be bijective. Then
\[
f^{-1} \circ f = \id_A
\quad\text{and}\quad
f \circ f^{-1} = \id_B.
\]
Conversely, a function admits an inverse iff it is bijective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f : A \to B$ be bijective. Then
   > \[
   > f^{-1} \circ f = \id_A
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > f \circ f^{-1} = \id_B.
   > \]
   > Conversely, a function admits an inverse iff it is bijective.

items.title: Inverse of a Composition
items.statement:
Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$ be bijective. Then $g \circ f$ is
bijective and
\[
(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$ be bijective. Then $g \circ f$ is
   > bijective and
   > \[
   > (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}.
   > \]

items.title: One-Sided Inverses and Function Properties
items.statement:
Let $f : A \to B$.
- [label=(\roman*)]
- $f$ has a left inverse $\iff$ $f$ is injective (and $A \neq \varnothing$ or $A=B=\varnothing$).
- $f$ has a right inverse $\iff$ $f$ is surjective.
- If $f$ has both a left inverse $g$ and a right inverse $h$, then $g = h$
and $f$ is bijective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f : A \to B$.
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - $f$ has a left inverse $\iff$ $f$ is injective (and $A \neq \varnothing$ or $A=B=\varnothing$).
   > - $f$ has a right inverse $\iff$ $f$ is surjective.
   > - If $f$ has both a left inverse $g$ and a right inverse $h$, then $g = h$
   > and $f$ is bijective.

items.title: Preimages Preserve Set Operations
items.statement:
Let $f : A \to B$ and $S, T \subseteq B$. Then
- [label=(\roman*)]
- $f^{-1}(S \cup T) = f^{-1}(S) \cup f^{-1}(T)$,
- $f^{-1}(S \cap T) = f^{-1}(S) \cap f^{-1}(T)$,
- $f^{-1}(S \setminus T) = f^{-1}(S) \setminus f^{-1}(T)$,
- $f^{-1}(S^c) = (f^{-1}(S))^c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f : A \to B$ and $S, T \subseteq B$. Then
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - $f^{-1}(S \cup T) = f^{-1}(S) \cup f^{-1}(T)$,
   > - $f^{-1}(S \cap T) = f^{-1}(S) \cap f^{-1}(T)$,
   > - $f^{-1}(S \setminus T) = f^{-1}(S) \setminus f^{-1}(T)$,
   > - $f^{-1}(S^c) = (f^{-1}(S))^c$.

items.title: Images and Set Operations
items.statement:
Let $f : A \to B$ and $S, T \subseteq A$. Then
- [label=(\roman*)]
- $f(S \cup T) = f(S) \cup f(T)$,
- $f(S \cap T) \subseteq f(S) \cap f(T)$,
- $f(S \setminus T) \supseteq f(S) \setminus f(T)$.
Equality holds in (ii) and (iii) for all $S,T$ iff $f$ is injective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f : A \to B$ and $S, T \subseteq A$. Then
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - $f(S \cup T) = f(S) \cup f(T)$,
   > - $f(S \cap T) \subseteq f(S) \cap f(T)$,
   > - $f(S \setminus T) \supseteq f(S) \setminus f(T)$.
   > Equality holds in (ii) and (iii) for all $S,T$ iff $f$ is injective.

items.title: Image--Preimage Adjunction
items.statement:
Let $f:A\to B$, let $S\subseteq A$, and let $T\subseteq B$. Then
\[
S\subseteq f^{-1}(f(S)),
\qquad
f(f^{-1}(T))\subseteq T.
\]
Moreover, $S=f^{-1}(f(S))$ for every $S\subseteq A$ iff $f$ is injective, and
$f(f^{-1}(T))=T$ for every $T\subseteq B$ iff $f$ is surjective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f:A\to B$, let $S\subseteq A$, and let $T\subseteq B$. Then
   > \[
   > S\subseteq f^{-1}(f(S)),
   > \qquad
   > f(f^{-1}(T))\subseteq T.
   > \]
   > Moreover, $S=f^{-1}(f(S))$ for every $S\subseteq A$ iff $f$ is injective, and
   > $f(f^{-1}(T))=T$ for every $T\subseteq B$ iff $f$ is surjective.

items.title: Functional Relation Characterization of Functions
items.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets, and let $R\subseteq A\times B$. Then $R$ is a
function from $A$ to $B$ if and only if
\[
\forall a\in A\,\exists! b\in B,\quad (a,b)\in R.
\]
Equivalently, $R$ is a function from $A$ to $B$ if and only if $R$ is total
on $A$ and functional from $A$ to $B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A$ and $B$ be sets, and let $R\subseteq A\times B$. Then $R$ is a
   > function from $A$ to $B$ if and only if
   > \[
   > \forall a\in A\,\exists! b\in B,\quad (a,b)\in R.
   > \]
   > Equivalently, $R$ is a function from $A$ to $B$ if and only if $R$ is total
   > on $A$ and functional from $A$ to $B$.

items.title: Partial Functions Are Functional Relations
items.statement:
For sets $A$ and $B$ and a relation $R\subseteq A\times B$, $R$ is a partial
function from $A$ to $B$ if and only if $R$ is functional from $A$ to $B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For sets $A$ and $B$ and a relation $R\subseteq A\times B$, $R$ is a partial
   > function from $A$ to $B$ if and only if $R$ is functional from $A$ to $B$.

items.title: One-to-Many Relations Are Not Functional
items.statement:
If $R\subseteq A\times B$ is one-to-many, then $R$ is not functional from $A$
to $B$. Consequently, $R$ is not a function from $A$ to $B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $R\subseteq A\times B$ is one-to-many, then $R$ is not functional from $A$
   > to $B$. Consequently, $R$ is not a function from $A$ to $B$.

items.title: One-One Relations and Converse Functionality
items.statement:
Let $f:A\to B$ be a function, identified with its graph
$G_f\subseteq A\times B$. Then $f$ is injective if and only if the converse
relation $G_f^{-1}\subseteq B\times A$ is functional from $B$ to $A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f:A\to B$ be a function, identified with its graph
   > $G_f\subseteq A\times B$. Then $f$ is injective if and only if the converse
   > relation $G_f^{-1}\subseteq B\times A$ is functional from $B$ to $A$.

items.title: Bijections Have Unique Correspondence Both Ways
items.statement:
Let $f:A\to B$ be a function. Then $f$ is bijective if and only if
\[
\forall a\in A\,\exists! b\in B,\quad f(a)=b,
\]
and
\[
\forall b\in B\,\exists! a\in A,\quad f(a)=b.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f:A\to B$ be a function. Then $f$ is bijective if and only if
   > \[
   > \forall a\in A\,\exists! b\in B,\quad f(a)=b,
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > \forall b\in B\,\exists! a\in A,\quad f(a)=b.
   > \]

items.title: Complete preorder extension
items.statement:
For any nonempty set $X$ and preorder $\succsim$ on $X$, there exists a
complete preorder that is an extension of $\succsim$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any nonempty set $X$ and preorder $\succsim$ on $X$, there exists a
   > complete preorder that is an extension of $\succsim$.

items.title: Duality Principle for Posets
items.statement:
Let $\Phi$ be any first-order statement about a poset $(A, \leq)$ expressed
using only the relation $\leq$. Let $\Phi^*$ be the statement obtained from
$\Phi$ by replacing every occurrence of $\leq$ with $\geq$ (equivalently,
working in the dual poset). Then:
\[
 (A, \leq) \models \Phi
 \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
 (A, \geq) \models \Phi.
\]
In particular, if $\Phi$ is a theorem about all posets, then so is $\Phi^*$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\Phi$ be any first-order statement about a poset $(A, \leq)$ expressed
   > using only the relation $\leq$. Let $\Phi^*$ be the statement obtained from
   > $\Phi$ by replacing every occurrence of $\leq$ with $\geq$ (equivalently,
   > working in the dual poset). Then:
   > \[
   >  (A, \leq) \models \Phi
   >  \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
   >  (A, \geq) \models \Phi.
   > \]
   > In particular, if $\Phi$ is a theorem about all posets, then so is $\Phi^*$.

items.title: $\leq_f$ is always a preorder
items.statement:
For any function $f : A \to B$ and partial order $(B, \leq')$, the relation
$\leq_f$ is a preorder on $A$: it is reflexive and transitive.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any function $f : A \to B$ and partial order $(B, \leq')$, the relation
   > $\leq_f$ is a preorder on $A$: it is reflexive and transitive.

items.title: $\leq_f$ is a partial order iff $f$ is injective
items.statement:
Let $(B, \leq')$ be a partially ordered set and $f : A \to B$.
The induced order $\leq_f
$ is a partial order on $A$ if and only if
$f$ is injective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(B, \leq')$ be a partially ordered set and $f : A \to B$.
   > The induced order $\leq_f
   > $ is a partial order on $A$ if and only if
   > $f$ is injective.

items.title: Order embeddings are injective
items.statement: Every order embedding $f : (A, \leq) \to (B, \leq')$ is injective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every order embedding $f : (A, \leq) \to (B, \leq')$ is injective.

items.title: Order embedding is isomorphism onto image
items.statement:
If $f : (A, \leq) \to (B, \leq')$ is an order embedding, then $f$ is an
order isomorphism from $(A, \leq)$ to the suborder $(f(A), \leq'_{f(A)})$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $f : (A, \leq) \to (B, \leq')$ is an order embedding, then $f$ is an
   > order isomorphism from $(A, \leq)$ to the suborder $(f(A), \leq'_{f(A)})$.

items.title: Uniqueness of Supremum and Infimum
items.statement:
Let $(A, \leq)$ be a poset and $S \subseteq A$. If $\sup S$ exists, it is
unique. If $\inf S$ exists, it is unique.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(A, \leq)$ be a poset and $S \subseteq A$. If $\sup S$ exists, it is
   > unique. If $\inf S$ exists, it is unique.

items.title: Characterisation of Supremum
items.statement:
Let $(A, \leq)$ be a poset, $S \subseteq A$, and $u^* \in A$. Then
$u^* = \sup S$ if and only if:
- [label=(\roman*)]
- $u^*$ is an upper bound of $S$; and
- for every $v \in A$ with $v < u^*$, there exists $s \in S$ with
 $v < s$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(A, \leq)$ be a poset, $S \subseteq A$, and $u^* \in A$. Then
   > $u^* = \sup S$ if and only if:
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - $u^*$ is an upper bound of $S$; and
   > - for every $v \in A$ with $v < u^*$, there exists $s \in S$ with
   >  $v < s$.

items.title: Duality of Supremum and Infimum
items.statement:
Let $(A, \leq)$ be a poset and $S \subseteq A$. Then
$\inf_{(A,\leq)} S = \sup_{(A,\geq)} S$,
where $(A,\geq)$ denotes the dual poset.

In particular: if every nonempty bounded-above subset of $(A,\leq)$ has a
supremum, then every nonempty bounded-below subset of $(A,\leq)$ has an
infimum.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(A, \leq)$ be a poset and $S \subseteq A$. Then
   > $\inf_{(A,\leq)} S = \sup_{(A,\geq)} S$,
   > where $(A,\geq)$ denotes the dual poset.
   >
   > In particular: if every nonempty bounded-above subset of $(A,\leq)$ has a
   > supremum, then every nonempty bounded-below subset of $(A,\leq)$ has an
   > infimum.

items.title: Strict Order Induced by a Linear Order
items.statement:
If $\leq$ is a linear order on $S$ and
\[
x<y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; (x\leq y\land x\neq y),
\]
then $<$ is a strict linear order on $S$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\leq$ is a linear order on $S$ and
   > \[
   > x<y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; (x\leq y\land x\neq y),
   > \]
   > then $<$ is a strict linear order on $S$.

items.title: Linear Order Induced by a Strict Linear Order
items.statement:
If $<$ is a strict linear order on $S$ and
\[
x\leq y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; (x<y\lor x=y),
\]
then $\leq$ is a linear order on $S$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $<$ is a strict linear order on $S$ and
   > \[
   > x\leq y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; (x<y\lor x=y),
   > \]
   > then $\leq$ is a linear order on $S$.

items.title: Trichotomy for Linear Orders
items.statement:
If $\leq$ is a linear order on $S$, then for all $x,y\in S$, exactly one of
the following holds:
\[
x<y,\qquad x=y,\qquad y<x.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\leq$ is a linear order on $S$, then for all $x,y\in S$, exactly one of
   > the following holds:
   > \[
   > x<y,\qquad x=y,\qquad y<x.
   > \]

items.title: Order Isomorphisms Preserve and Reflect Order
items.statement:
Let $(A,\leq_A)$ and $(B,\leq_B)$ be ordered sets. If $f:A\to B$ is an order
isomorphism, then for all $x,y\in A$,
\[
x\leq_A y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; f(x)\leq_B f(y).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(A,\leq_A)$ and $(B,\leq_B)$ be ordered sets. If $f:A\to B$ is an order
   > isomorphism, then for all $x,y\in A$,
   > \[
   > x\leq_A y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; f(x)\leq_B f(y).
   > \]

items.title: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable
items.statement: The set $\mathbb{Q}$ of rational numbers is countable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The set $\mathbb{Q}$ of rational numbers is countable.

items.title: Countable union of countable sets is countable
items.statement:
Let $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a countable family of countable sets.
Then $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n$ is countable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a countable family of countable sets.
   > Then $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n$ is countable.

items.title: $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
items.statement: The set $\mathbb{R}$ of real numbers is not countable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The set $\mathbb{R}$ of real numbers is not countable.

items.title: Cantor's Theorem
items.statement:
For any set $A$, there is no surjection $A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$. In
particular, $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any set $A$, there is no surjection $A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$. In
   > particular, $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.

items.title: Schr\"{o}der--Bernstein Theorem
items.statement:
If $|A| \leq |B|$ and $|B| \leq |A|$, then $A \sim B$.

Equivalently: if there exist injections $f : A \hookrightarrow B$ and
$g : B \hookrightarrow A$, then there exists a bijection $h : A \to B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $|A| \leq |B|$ and $|B| \leq |A|$, then $A \sim B$.
   >
   > Equivalently: if there exist injections $f : A \hookrightarrow B$ and
   > $g : B \hookrightarrow A$, then there exists a bijection $h : A \to B$.

items.title: Equality Is the Finest Equivalence
items.statement:
Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $A$. For all $a,b\in A$,
\[
a=b \Longrightarrow a\sim b.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $A$. For all $a,b\in A$,
   > \[
   > a=b \Longrightarrow a\sim b.
   > \]

items.title: Equivalence Classes Partition the Domain
items.statement:
The equivalence classes of an equivalence relation on $A$ are nonempty, cover
$A$, and are pairwise disjoint.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The equivalence classes of an equivalence relation on $A$ are nonempty, cover
   > $A$, and are pairwise disjoint.

items.title: Representatives Related iff Classes Equal
items.statement:
\[
a\sim b \Longleftrightarrow [a]=[b].
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > a\sim b \Longleftrightarrow [a]=[b].
   > \]

items.title: Projection Is Surjective
items.statement: The canonical projection $\pi:A\to A/{\sim}$ is surjective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The canonical projection $\pi:A\to A/{\sim}$ is surjective.

items.title: Projection Identifies Exactly the Equivalent Elements
items.statement:
For all $a,b\in A$,
\[
\pi(a)=\pi(b)\Longleftrightarrow a\sim b.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all $a,b\in A$,
   > \[
   > \pi(a)=\pi(b)\Longleftrightarrow a\sim b.
   > \]

items.title: Existence of a Quotient
items.statement:
For any equivalence relation $\sim$ on $A$, the quotient set $A/{\sim}$ exists
as the set of equivalence classes, and the canonical projection
\[
\pi:A\to A/{\sim}
\]
is well-defined.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any equivalence relation $\sim$ on $A$, the quotient set $A/{\sim}$ exists
   > as the set of equivalence classes, and the canonical projection
   > \[
   > \pi:A\to A/{\sim}
   > \]
   > is well-defined.

items.title: Respect Splits
items.statement:
A binary operation $O$ respects $\sim$ if and only if it respects $\sim$ on
the left and on the right.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A binary operation $O$ respects $\sim$ if and only if it respects $\sim$ on
   > the left and on the right.

items.title: Induced Operation on a Quotient
items.statement:
If $O:A\times A\to A$ respects $\sim$, then
\[
[a]\mathbin{\overline{O}}[b]:=[a\mathbin{O}b]
\]
defines a well-defined binary operation on $A/{\sim}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $O:A\times A\to A$ respects $\sim$, then
   > \[
   > [a]\mathbin{\overline{O}}[b]:=[a\mathbin{O}b]
   > \]
   > defines a well-defined binary operation on $A/{\sim}$.

items.title: Induced Unary Operation
items.statement:
Let $f:A\to A$. If
\[
a\sim a'\Longrightarrow f(a)\sim f(a'),
\]
then
\[
\overline{f}([a]):=[f(a)]
\]
defines a well-defined unary operation on $A/{\sim}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f:A\to A$. If
   > \[
   > a\sim a'\Longrightarrow f(a)\sim f(a'),
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   > \overline{f}([a]):=[f(a)]
   > \]
   > defines a well-defined unary operation on $A/{\sim}$.

items.title: Induced Predicate on a Quotient
items.statement:
If $P$ respects $\sim$, then
\[
\overline{P}([a]):\Longleftrightarrow P(a)
\]
defines a well-defined predicate on $A/{\sim}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $P$ respects $\sim$, then
   > \[
   > \overline{P}([a]):\Longleftrightarrow P(a)
   > \]
   > defines a well-defined predicate on $A/{\sim}$.

items.title: Induced Relation on a Quotient
items.statement:
If $R$ respects $\sim$, then
\[
\overline{R}([a],[b]):\Longleftrightarrow R(a,b)
\]
defines a well-defined binary relation on $A/{\sim}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $R$ respects $\sim$, then
   > \[
   > \overline{R}([a],[b]):\Longleftrightarrow R(a,b)
   > \]
   > defines a well-defined binary relation on $A/{\sim}$.

items.title: Induced Map out of a Quotient
items.statement:
Let $g:A\to B$. If
\[
a\sim a'\Longrightarrow g(a)=g(a'),
\]
then there is a unique w
ell-defined map
\[
\overline{g}:A/{\sim}\to B
\]
such that
\[
\overline{g}([a])=g(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\overline{g}\circ\pi=g,
\]
where $\pi:A\to A/{\sim}$ is the canonical projection.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $g:A\to B$. If
   > \[
   > a\sim a'\Longrightarrow g(a)=g(a'),
   > \]
   > then there is a unique w
   > ell-defined map
   > \[
   > \overline{g}:A/{\sim}\to B
   > \]
   > such that
   > \[
   > \overline{g}([a])=g(a)
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > \overline{g}\circ\pi=g,
   > \]
   > where $\pi:A\to A/{\sim}$ is the canonical projection.

items.title: Induced Partial Operation on a Quotient
items.statement:
Let $D\subseteq A$ be saturated under $\sim$, meaning
\[
a\in D\land a\sim a'\Longrightarrow a'\in D.
\]
If $f:D\to A$ respects $\sim$ on $D$, then
\[
\overline{f}([a]):=[f(a)]
\]
is a well-defined partial operation on $A/{\sim}$ with domain
\[
D/{\sim}:=\{[a]\in A/{\sim}:a\in D\}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $D\subseteq A$ be saturated under $\sim$, meaning
   > \[
   > a\in D\land a\sim a'\Longrightarrow a'\in D.
   > \]
   > If $f:D\to A$ respects $\sim$ on $D$, then
   > \[
   > \overline{f}([a]):=[f(a)]
   > \]
   > is a well-defined partial operation on $A/{\sim}$ with domain
   > \[
   > D/{\sim}:=\{[a]\in A/{\sim}:a\in D\}.
   > \]

items.title: Representative Independence Is Necessary
items.statement:
If a rule on classes
\[
[a]\mathbin{\overline{O}}[b]:=[a\mathbin{O}b]
\]
is well-defined on $A/{\sim}$, then $O$ respects $\sim$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If a rule on classes
   > \[
   > [a]\mathbin{\overline{O}}[b]:=[a\mathbin{O}b]
   > \]
   > is well-defined on $A/{\sim}$, then $O$ respects $\sim$.

items.title: Distinct Equivalence Classes Are Disjoint
items.statement:
\[
[a]\ne[b] \Longrightarrow [a]\cap[b]=\emptyset.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > [a]\ne[b] \Longrightarrow [a]\cap[b]=\emptyset.
   > \]

items.title: Symmetry of Equality
items.statement:
\[
\forall x\,\forall y,\ (x=y \Longrightarrow y=x).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\forall y,\ (x=y \Longrightarrow y=x).
   > \]

items.title: Transitivity of Equality
items.statement:
\[
\forall x\,\forall y\,\forall z,\,
\bigl(x=y \land y=z \Longrightarrow x=z\bigr).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > \forall x\,\forall y\,\forall z,\,
   > \bigl(x=y \land y=z \Longrightarrow x=z\bigr).
   > \]

items.title: Equality Is an Equivalence Relation
items.statement: The equality relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The equality relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

items.title: Substitution Preserves Predicates
items.statement:
\[
x=y \Longrightarrow \bigl(P(x)\Longleftrightarrow P(y)\bigr).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > x=y \Longrightarrow \bigl(P(x)\Longleftrightarrow P(y)\bigr).
   > \]

items.title: Substitution Preserves Relations on the Left
items.statement:
\[
x=y \Longrightarrow \bigl(R(x,z)\Longleftrightarrow R(y,z)\bigr).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > x=y \Longrightarrow \bigl(R(x,z)\Longleftrightarrow R(y,z)\bigr).
   > \]

items.title: Substitution Preserves Relations on the Right
items.statement:
\[
x=y \Longrightarrow \bigl(R(z,x)\Longleftrightarrow R(z,y)\bigr).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > x=y \Longrightarrow \bigl(R(z,x)\Longleftrightarrow R(z,y)\bigr).
   > \]

items.title: Substitution Preserves Relations
items.statement:
\[
x=x' \land y=y' \Longrightarrow
\bigl(R(x,y)\Longleftrightarrow R(x',y')\bigr).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > x=x' \land y=y' \Longrightarrow
   > \bigl(R(x,y)\Longleftrightarrow R(x',y')\bigr).
   > \]

items.title: Substitution Preserves Functions
items.statement:
\[
x=y \Longrightarrow f(x)=f(y).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > x=y \Longrightarrow f(x)=f(y).
   > \]

items.title: Left Congruence for Operations
items.statement:
\[
x=x' \Longrightarrow x\mathbin{O}y=x'\mathbin{O}y.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > x=x' \Longrightarrow x\mathbin{O}y=x'\mathbin{O}y.
   > \]

items.title: Right Congruence for Operations
items.statement:
\[
y=y' \Longrightarrow x\mathbin{O}y=x\mathbin{O}y'.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > y=y' \Longrightarrow x\mathbin{O}y=x\mathbin{O}y'.
   > \]

items.title: Full Congruence for Operations
items.statement:
\[
x=x' \land y=y' \Longrightarrow x\mathbin{O}y=x'\mathbin{O}y'.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > x=x' \land y=y' \Longrightarrow x\mathbin{O}y=x'\mathbin{O}y'.
   > \]

items.title: Congruence with Respect to Equality Is Automatic
items.statement:
Every function, predicate, relation, and operation respects equality in its
displayed arguments.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every function, predicate, relation, and operation respects equality in its
   > displayed arguments.

items.title: General Commutativity
items.statement:
If $O$ is associative and commutative, then any finite reordering of
$x_1\mathbin{O}\cdots\mathbin{O}x_n$ has the same value.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $O$ is associative and commutative, then any finite reordering of
   > $x_1\mathbin{O}\cdots\mathbin{O}x_n$ has the same value.

items.title: Invertibility Implies Left Cancellation
items.statement:
In an associative operation with identity, invertible elements satisfy left
cancellation.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an associative operation with identity, invertible elements satisfy left
   > cancellation.

items.title: Invertibility Implies Right Cancellation
items.statement:
In an associative operation with identity, invertible elements satisfy right
cancellation.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an associative operation with identity, invertible elements satisfy right
   > cancellation.

items.title: Invertibility Implies Cancellation
items.statement:
In an associative operation with identity, invertible elements satisfy
two-sided cancellation.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an associative operation with identity, invertible elements satisfy
   > two-sided cancellation.

items.title: Left Respect
items.statement:
If a binary operation respects $\sim$, then
\[
a\sim a' \Longrightarrow a\mathbin{O}b\sim a'\mathbin{O}b.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If a binary operation respects $\sim$, then
   > \[
   > a\sim a' \Longrightarrow a\mathbin{O}b\sim a'\mathbin{O}b.
   > \]

items.title: Right Respect
items.statement:
If a binary operation respects $\sim$, then
\[
b\sim b' \Longrightarrow a\mathbin{O}b\sim a\mathbin{O}b'.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If a binary operation respects $\sim$, then
   > \[
   > b\sim b' \Longrightarrow a\mathbin{O}b\sim a\mathbin{O}b'.
   > \]

items.title: Induced Operation
items.statement:
The operation
\[
[a]\mathbin{\overline{O}}[b]:=[a\mathbin{O}b]
\]
on $A/{\sim}$ is well-defined if and only if $O$ respects $\sim$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The operation
   > \[
   > [a]\mathbin{\overline{O}}[b]:=[a\mathbin{O}b]
   > \]
   > on $A/{\sim}$ is well-defined if and only if $O$ respects $\sim$.

items.title: Left Zero Absorption
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and $0$ is the additive identity,
\[
0\cdot a=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and $0$ is the additive identity,
   > \[
   > 0\cdot a=0.
   > \]

items.title: Right Zero Absorption
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and $0$ is the additive identity,
\[
a\cdot 0=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and $0$ is the additive identity,
   > \[
   > a\cdot 0=0.
   > \]

items.title: Zero Absorption
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and $0$ is the additive identity,
\[
0\cdot a=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a\cdot 0=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and $0$ is the additive identity,
   > \[
   > 0\cdot a=0
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > a\cdot 0=0.
   > \]

items.title: Left Sign Rule
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
\[
(-a)\cdot b=-(a\cdot b).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
   > \[
   > (-a)\cdot b=-(a\cdot b).
   > \]

items.title: Right Sign Rule
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
\[
a\cdot(-b)=-(a\cdot b).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
   > \[
   > a\cdot(-b)=-(a\cdot b).
   > \]

items.title: Sign Rule
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
\[
(-a)\cdot b=-(a\cdot b)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a\cdot(-b)=-(a\cdot b).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
   > \[
   > (-a)\cdot b=-(a\cdot b)
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > a\cdot(-b)=-(a\cdot b).
   > \]

items.title: Negative One Rule
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
\[
(-1)\cdot a=-a.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
   > \[
   > (-1)\cdot a=-a.
   > \]

items.title: Product of Negatives
items.statement:
When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b)=a\cdot b.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > When multiplication distributes over addition and additive inverses exist,
   > \[
   > (-a)\cdot(-b)=a\cdot b.
   > \]

items.title: No Zero Divisors
items.statement:
In an arithmetic system with no nonzero zero divisors,
\[
a\cdot b=0 \Longrightarrow a=0 \lor b=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an arithmetic system with no nonzero zero divisors,
   > \[
   > a\cdot b=0 \Longrightarrow a=0 \lor b=0.
   > \]

items.title: Left and Right Identities Coincide
items.statement:
If $e_L$ is a left identity and $e_R$ is a right identity for the same
operation, then $e_L=e_R$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $e_L$ is a left identity and $e_R$ is a right identity for the same
   > operation, then $e_L=e_R$.

items.title: Uniqueness of Identity
items.statement: A two-sided identity for a binary operation is unique.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A two-sided identity for a binary operation is unique.

items.title: Left and Right Inverses Coincide
items.statement:
In an associative operation with identity, a left inverse and a right inverse
of the same element are equal.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an associative operation with identity, a left inverse and a right inverse
   > of the same element are equal.

items.title: Uniqueness of Inverse
items.statement: In an associative operation with identity, inverses are unique.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an associative operation with identity, inverses are unique.

items.title: Solvability and Inverses
items.statement:
For an associative operation with a two-sided identity, solvability is
equivalent to the existence of inverses.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For an associative operation with a two-sided identity, solvability is
   > equivalent to the existence of inverses.

items.title: Addition Preserves Order on the Left
items.statement:
\[
y<z \Longrightarrow x+y<x+z
\]
in ordered arithmetic systems where addition is strictly order-preserving.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > y<z \Longrightarrow x+y<x+z
   > \]
   > in ordered arithmetic systems where addition is strictly order-preserving.

items.title: Addition Preserves Order on the Right
items.statement:
\[
y<z \Longrightarrow y+x<z+x
\]
in ordered arithmetic systems where addition is strictly order-preserving.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > y<z \Longrightarrow y+x<z+x
   > \]
   > in ordered arithmetic systems where addition is strictly order-preserving.

items.title: Addition Preserves Order
items.statement:
In ordered arithmetic systems where addition is strictly order-preserving,
addition preserves order on both sides.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In ordered arithmetic systems where addition is strictly order-preserving,
   > addition preserves order on both sides.

items.title: Multiplication Preserves Order on the Left
items.statement:
\[
0<x \land y<z \Longrightarrow x\cdot y<x\cdot z
\]
in ordered arithmetic systems where multiplication by positive elements is
strictly order-preserving.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > 0<x \land y<z \Longrightarrow x\cdot y<x\cdot z
   > \]
   > in ordered arithmetic systems where multiplication by positive elements is
   > strictly order-preserving.

items.title: Multiplication Preserves Order on the Right
items.statement:
\[
0<x \land y<z \Longrightarrow y\cdot x<z\cdot x
\]
in ordered arithmetic systems where multiplication by positive elements is
strictly order-preserving.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > 0<x \land y<z \Longrightarrow y\cdot x<z\cdot x
   > \]
   > in ordered arithmetic systems where multiplication by positive elements is
   > strictly order-preserving.

items.title: Multiplication Preserves Order
items.statement:
In ordered arithmetic systems where multiplication by positive elements is
strictly order-preserving, multiplication preserves order on both sides.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In ordered arithmetic systems where multiplication by positive elements is
   > strictly order-preserving, multiplication preserves order on both sides.

items.title: Composition of Homomorphisms
items.statement: The composition of two homomorphisms is a homomorphism.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The composition of two homomorphisms is a homomorphism.

items.title: Identity Map Is a Homomorphism
items.statement:
The identity map on a structure is a homomorphism from that structure to
itself.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The identity map on a structure is a homomorphism from that structure to
   > itself.

items.title: Congruence Modulo an Integer Is an Equivalence Relation
items.statement:
For each positive integer \(n\), congruence modulo \(n\) is an equivalence
relation on \(\mathbb{Z}\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For each positive integer \(n\), congruence modulo \(n\) is an equivalence
   > relation on \(\mathbb{Z}\).

items.title: Modular Addition and Multiplication Are Well-Defined
items.statement:
For each positive integer \(n\), addition and multiplication modulo \(n\) are
well-defined operations on \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For each positive integer \(n\), addition and multiplication modulo \(n\) are
   > well-defined operations on \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\).

items.title: \(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\) Has Zero Divisors
items.statement:
In \(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\), the nonzero class \([2]_4\) satisfies
\[
[2]_4\cdot[2]_4=[0]_4.
\]
Therefore \(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\) is not a field.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In \(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\), the nonzero class \([2]_4\) satisfies
   > \[
   > [2]_4\cdot[2]_4=[0]_4.
   > \]
   > Therefore \(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\) is not a field.

items.title: The Two-Element System Is a Field
items.statement: The two-element number system \(\mathbb{F}_2\) is a field.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The two-element number system \(\mathbb{F}_2\) is a field.

items.title: The Two-Element System Is Not an Ordered Field
items.statement:
There is no order on \(\mathbb{B}_2\) that makes
\(\mathbb{F}_2\) an ordered field.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > There is no order on \(\mathbb{B}_2\) that makes
   > \(\mathbb{F}_2\) an ordered field.

items.title: \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) Is the Two-Element System
items.statement:
The finite modular number system \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) has exactly two
classes, \([0]_2\) and \([1]_2\), and its addition and multiplication tables
are the tables of \(\mathbb{F}_2\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The finite modular number system \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) has exactly two
   > classes, \([0]_2\) and \([1]_2\), and its addition and multiplication tables
   > are the tables of \(\mathbb{F}_2\).

items.title: Induction Principle for a Peano System
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\varphi(1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
   > If
   > \[
   > \varphi(1)
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > \forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))),
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   > \forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
   > \]

items.title: Strong Induction on a Peano System
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\forall n \in P\;
\bigl(\forall k \in P\;(k < n \Longrightarrow \varphi(k))\bigr)
\Longrightarrow \varphi(n),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
   > If
   > \[
   > \forall n \in P\;
   > \bigl(\forall k \in P\;(k < n \Longrightarrow \varphi(k))\bigr)
   > \Longrightarrow \varphi(n),
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   > \forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
   > \]

items.title: Minimality of a Peano System
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. If $A\subseteq P$ contains $1$ and is closed
under successor, then $A=P$.
\[
\bigl(1\in A \land
\forall n\in P\;(n\in A \Longrightarrow S(n)\in A)\bigr)
\Longrightarrow A=P.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. If $A\subseteq P$ contains $1$ and is closed
   > under successor, then $A=P$.
   > \[
   > \bigl(1\in A \land
   > \forall n\in P\;(n\in A \Longrightarrow S(n)\in A)\bigr)
   > \Longrightarrow A=P.
   > \]

items.title: Every Element Is Either $1$ or a Successor
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, either $x=1$ or there
exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, either $x=1$ or there
   > exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.

items.title: Successor Inequality Reflection
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,b \in P$, if $a \neq b$, then
$S(a)\neq S(b)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,b \in P$, if $a \neq b$, then
   > $S(a)\neq S(b)$.

items.title: Non-One Elements Have a Predecessor
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, if $x \neq 1$, then
there exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, if $x \neq 1$, then
   > there exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.

items.title: Predecessor Existence and Uniqueness Away from $1$
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $x \in P$ with $x \neq 1$. Then
there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $x \in P$ with $x \neq 1$. Then
   > there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.

items.title: Unique Predecessor Characterization Away from $1$
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, $x \neq 1$ if and
only if there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, $x \neq 1$ if and
   > only if there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.

items.title: The Distinguished Element Is the Unique Non-Successor
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. An element $x \in P$ is not a successor of
any element of $P$ if and only if $x=1$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. An element $x \in P$ is not a successor of
   > any element of $P$ if and only if $x=1$.

items.title: No Object Is Its Own Successor
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $n \in P$,
\[
S(n) \neq n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $n \in P$,
   > \[
   > S(n) \neq n.
   > \]

items.title: Consistency of the Minimal Iterator Relation
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$. Then $R^*$ is an
iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
   > $R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$. Then $R^*$ is an
   > iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$.

items.title: Forced Values Are Unique
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. If $(n,w_0)\in R^*$ and
$(n,w_1)\in R^*$, then $w_0=w_1$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
   > $R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. If $(n,w_0)\in R^*$ and
   > $(n,w_1)\in R^*$, then $w_0=w_1$.

items.title: Determinism of the Minimal Iterator Relation
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. For each $n\in P$, there is at most one
$w\in W$ such that $(n,w)\in R^*$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
   > $R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. For each $n\in P$, there is at most one
   > $w\in W$ such that $(n,w)\in R^*$.

items.title: Completeness of the Minimal Iterator Relation
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. For each $n\in P$, there exists
$w\in W$ such that $(n,w)\in R^*$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
   > $R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. For each $n\in P$, there exists
   > $w\in W$ such that $(n,w)\in R^*$.

items.title: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. If
$f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. If
   > $f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
   > \[
   > f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > \forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
   > \]
   > then $f=h$.

items.title: Existence of an Iterator Function
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
Then there exists a function $f:P\to W$ such that
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
   > Then there exists a function $f:P\to W$ such that
   > \[
   > f(1)=c
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
   > \]

items.title: Peano Iterator Theorem
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
Then there exists a unique function $f:P\to W$ such that
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
   > Then there exists a unique function $f:P\to W$ such that
   > \[
   > f(1)=c
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
   > \]

items.title: Iterator Base Clause
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$f$ be the iterator-generated function determined by $(W,c,g)$. Then
\[
f(1)=c.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
   > $f$ be the iterator-generated function determined by $(W,c,g)$. Then
   > \[
   > f(1)=c.
   > \]

items.title: Iterator Successor Clause
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$f$ be the iterator-generated function determined by $(W,c,g)$. Then
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
   > $f$ be the iterator-generated function determined by $(W,c,g)$. Then
   > \[
   > \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
   > \]

items.title: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
\[
F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]
and
\[
F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
   > suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
   > If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
   > \[
   > F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
   > \qquad
   > G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
   > \]
   > for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.

items.title: Uniqueness of General Recursive Functions
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi:P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. If $f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=\Phi(n,h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
   > $\Phi:P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. If $f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
   > \[
   > f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n)))
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > \forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=\Phi(n,h(n))),
   > \]
   > then $f=h$.

items.title: General Recursion by State Encoding
items.statement:

$H:P\to P\times W$ such that
\[
H(1)=(1,c)
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;
\bigl(H(S(n))=(S(\pi_1(H(n))),\Phi(\pi_1(H(n)),\pi_2(H(n))))\bigr).
\]

items.title: General Recursion Theorem
items.statement:

\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n))).

items.title: Uniqueness of Peano Systems up to Isomorphism
items.statement:
Let $(P,S_P,1_P)$ and $(Q,S_Q,1_Q)$ be Peano systems. Then there exists a
unique bijection $\theta:P\to Q$ such that
\[
\theta(1_P)=1_Q
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(\theta(S_P(n))=S_Q(\theta(n))).
\]
Thus any two Peano systems are isomorphic.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S_P,1_P)$ and $(Q,S_Q,1_Q)$ be Peano systems. Then there exists a
   > unique bijection $\theta:P\to Q$ such that

   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > \forall n\in P\;(\theta(S_P(n))=S_Q(\theta(n))).
   > \]
   > Thus any two Peano systems are isomorphic.

items.title: Addition Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m+n \coloneqq f_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

items.title: $\mathbb{N}$ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
- \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
- \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
   > - \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
   > - \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
   >  $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
   > - \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
   > - \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
   > - \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.

items.title: $\mathbb{N}$ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
 $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
- \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
 $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
   > - \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
   > - \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
   >  $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
   > - \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
   >  $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
   > - \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
   >  $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
   > Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.

 \[
 a \cdot (b+c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c).
 \]

   >  \]

items.title: Induction from an Arbitrary Base
items.statement:

predicate on $P$. If
\[
\varphi(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;\bigl(n \ge m \land \varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))\bigr),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\bigl(n \ge m \Longrightarrow \varphi(n)\bigr).
\]

items.title: Natural-Number Order Is Total
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b \in P$,
\[
a \le b
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
b \le a.
\]
Consequently $\le$ is a total order on $P$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b \in P$,
   > \[
   > a \le b
   > \qquad\text{or}\qquad
   > b \le a.
   > \]
   > Consequently $\le$ is a total order on $P$.

items.title: Exponentiation Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
h_a:P\to P
\]
such that
\[
h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(a,n)\longmapsto a^n\coloneqq h_a(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a \in P$, there exists a unique
   > function
   > \[
   > h_a:P\to P
   > \]
   > such that
   > \[
   > h_a(1)=a
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > \forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
   > \]
   > Consequently the rule
   > \[
   > (a,n)\longmapsto a^n\coloneqq h_a(n)
   > \]
   > defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

items.title: Exponent Sum Law
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,m,n \in P$,
\[
a^{m+n} = a^m \cdot a^n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,m,n \in P$,
   > \[
   > a^{m+n} = a^m \cdot a^n.
   > \]

items.title: Exponent Product Law
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,b,n \in P$,
\[
(a \cdot b)^n = a^n \cdot b^n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,b,n \in P$,
   > \[
   > (a \cdot b)^n = a^n \cdot b^n.
   > \]

items.title: Exponent Power Law
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,m,n \in P$,
\[
(a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,m,n \in P$,
   > \[
   > (a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}.
   > \]

items.title: Powers with Common Exponent Preserve Strict Order
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,n \in P$,
\[
a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
a^n<b^n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,n \in P$,
   > \[
   > a<b
   > \Longleftrightarrow
   > a^n<b^n.
   > \]

items.title: Powers with Common Base Preserve Strict Order
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,m,n \in P$,
\[
a^m<a^n
\Longleftrightarrow
1<a \land m<n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,m,n \in P$,
   > \[
   > a^m<a^n
   > \Longleftrightarrow
   > 1<a \land m<n.
   > \]

items.title: $n < 2^n$ for All $n \in \mathbb{N}$
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $2 \coloneqq S(1)$. For every $n \in P$,
\[
n < 2^n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $2 \coloneqq S(1)$. For every $n \in P$,
   > \[
   > n < 2^n.
   > \]

items.title: Well-Ordering Principle
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
element with respect to the order $\le$ on $P$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
   > element with respect to the order $\le$ on $P$.

items.title: Induction, Strong Induction, and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent
items.statement:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
- The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
 $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
 for all $n \in P$.
- The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
 if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
 $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
- The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
 element with respect to $\le$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
   > are equivalent:
   > - The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
   >  $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
   >  for all $n \in P$.
   > - The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
   >  if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
   >  $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
   > - The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
   >  element with respect to $\le$.

items.title: Zero Is an Additive Identity on $\mathbb{W}$
items.statement:
For every $a\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
0+_{\mathbb{W}}a=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a+_{\mathbb{W}}0=a.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a\in\mathbb{W}$,
   > \[
   > 0+_{\mathbb{W}}a=a
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > a+_{\mathbb{W}}0=a.
   > \]

items.title: Addition on $\mathbb{W}$ Is Associative
items.statement:
For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
(a+_{\mathbb{W}}b)+_{\mathbb{W}}c
=
a+_{\mathbb{W}}(b+_{\mathbb{W}}c).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb{W}$,
   > \[
   > (a+_{\mathbb{W}}b)+_{\mathbb{W}}c
   > =
   > a+_{\mathbb{W}}(b+_{\mathbb{W}}c).
   > \]

items.title: Addition on $\mathbb{W}$ Is Commutative
items.statement:
For all $a,b\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
a+_{\mathbb{W}}b=b+_{\mathbb{W}}a.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all $a,b\in\mathbb{W}$,
   > \[
   > a+_{\mathbb{W}}b=b+_{\mathbb{W}}a.
   > \]

items.title: $(\mathbb{W},+,0)$ Is a Commutative Monoid
items.statement: The structure $(\mathbb{W},+_{\mathbb{W}},0)$ is a commutative monoid.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The structure $(\mathbb{W},+_{\mathbb{W}},0)$ is a commutative monoid.

items.title: One Is a Multiplicative Identity on $\mathbb{W}$
items.statement:
For every $a\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
1\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}a=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}1=a.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a\in\mathbb{W}$,
   > \[
   > 1\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}a=a
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}1=a.
   > \]

items.title: Zero Is Absorbing for Multiplication on $\mathbb{W}$
items.statement:
For every $a\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
0\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}a=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}0=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a\in\mathbb{W}$,
   > \[
   > 0\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}a=0
   > \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   > a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}0=0.
   > \]

items.title: Multiplication on $\mathbb{W}$ Is Associative
items.statement:
For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
(a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}b)\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}c
=
a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}(b\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}c).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb{W}$,
   > \[
   > (a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}b)\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}c
   > =

items.title: Multiplication on $\mathbb{W}$ Is Commutative
items.statement:
For all $a,b\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}b=b\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}a.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all $a,b\in\mathbb{W}$,
   > \[
   > a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}b=b\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}a.
   > \]

items.title: $(\mathbb{W},\cdot,1)$ Is a Commutative Monoid
items.statement: The structure $(\mathbb{W},\cdot_{\mathbb{W}},1)$ is a commutative monoid.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The structure $(\mathbb{W},\cdot_{\mathbb{W}},1)$ is a commutative monoid.

items.title: Multiplication Distributes over Addition on $\mathbb{W}$
items.statement:
For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb{W}$,
\[
a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}(b+_{\mathbb{W}}c)
=
(a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}b)+_{\mathbb{W}}(a\cdot_{\mathbb{W}}c).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb{W}$,
