items.title: Union Preserves Upper Bounds
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u_A$ is an upper bound of $A$ and
$u_B$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $\max\{u_A,u_B\}$ is an upper bound
of $A\cup B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u_A$ is an upper bound of $A$ and
   > $u_B$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $\max\{u_A,u_B\}$ is an upper bound
   > of $A\cup B$.

items.title: Union Preserves Lower Bounds
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $\ell_A$ is a lower bound of $A$ and
$\ell_B$ is a lower bound of $B$, then $\min\{\ell_A,\ell_B\}$ is a lower
bound of $A\cup B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $\ell_A$ is a lower bound of $A$ and
   > $\ell_B$ is a lower bound of $B$, then $\min\{\ell_A,\ell_B\}$ is a lower
   > bound of $A\cup B$.

items.title: Subsets Preserve Upper Bounds
items.statement:
Let $C\subseteq A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $A$,
then $u$ is an upper bound of $C$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $C\subseteq A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $A$,
   > then $u$ is an upper bound of $C$.

items.title: Union Is Bounded Above Exactly When Both Pieces Are
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty. Then $A\cup B$ is bounded above
if and only if $A$ is bounded above and $B$ is bounded above.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty. Then $A\cup B$ is bounded above
   > if and only if $A$ is bounded above and $B$ is bounded above.

items.title: Subsets Preserve Lower Bounds
items.statement:
Let $C\subseteq A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $\ell$ is a lower bound of $A$,
then $\ell$ is a lower bound of $C$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $C\subseteq A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $\ell$ is a lower bound of $A$,
   > then $\ell$ is a lower bound of $C$.

items.title: Union Is Bounded Below Exactly When Both Pieces Are
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty. Then $A\cup B$ is bounded below
if and only if $A$ is bounded below and $B$ is bounded below.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty. Then $A\cup B$ is bounded below
   > if and only if $A$ is bounded below and $B$ is bounded below.

items.title: Union Is Bounded Exactly When Both Pieces Are
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty. Then $A\cup B$ is bounded if and
only if $A$ is bounded and $B$ is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty. Then $A\cup B$ is bounded if and
   > only if $A$ is bounded and $B$ is bounded.

items.title: Intersections Inherit Bounds
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Every upper bound of $A$ is an upper bound
of $A\cap B$, and every lower bound of $A$ is a lower bound of $A\cap B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Every upper bound of $A$ is an upper bound
   > of $A\cap B$, and every lower bound of $A$ is a lower bound of $A\cap B$.

items.title: Differences Inherit Bounds
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Every upper bound of $A$ is an upper bound
of $A\setminus B$, and every lower bound of $A$ is a lower bound of
$A\setminus B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Every upper bound of $A$ is an upper bound
   > of $A\setminus B$, and every lower bound of $A$ is a lower bound of
   > $A\setminus B$.

items.title: Complements Inherit Ambient Bounds
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq E\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, and take complements relative to
$E$. Every upper bound of $E$ is an upper bound of $E\setminus A$, and
every lower bound of $E$ is a lower bound of $E\setminus A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq E\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, and take complements relative to
   > $E$. Every upper bound of $E$ is an upper bound of $E\setminus A$, and
   > every lower bound of $E$ is a lower bound of $E\setminus A$.

items.title: Supremum Strict Upper Approximation
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
$s=\sup A$. If $u<s$, then there exists $a\in A$ such that
\[
u<a\le s.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
   > $s=\sup A$. If $u<s$, then there exists $a\in A$ such that
   > \[
   > u<a\le s.
   > \]

items.title: Infimum Strict Lower Approximation
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$t=\inf A$. If $t<v$, then there exists $a\in A$ such that
\[
t\le a<v.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
   > $t=\inf A$. If $t<v$, then there exists $a\in A$ such that
   > \[
   > t\le a<v.
   > \]

items.title: Uniqueness of the Maximum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
$m,n\in S$ are both maxima of $A$, then $m=n$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
   > $m,n\in S$ are both maxima of $A$, then $m=n$.

items.title: Uniqueness of the Minimum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
$m,n\in S$ are both minima of $A$, then $m=n$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
   > $m,n\in S$ are both minima of $A$, then $m=n$.

items.title: Minimum Implies Infimum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
$m=\min A$, then $m=\inf A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
   > $m=\min A$, then $m=\inf A$.

items.title: Supremum in the Set is the Maximum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
$s=\sup A$ and $s\in A$, then $s=\max A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
   > $s=\sup A$ and $s\in A$, then $s=\max A$.

items.title: Infimum in the Set is the Minimum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
$i=\inf A$ and $i\in A$, then $i=\min A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
   > $i=\inf A$ and $i\in A$, then $i=\min A$.

items.title: Uniqueness of the Supremum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
$s,t\in S$ are both suprema of $A$, then $s=t$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
   > $s,t\in S$ are both suprema of $A$, then $s=t$.

items.title: Uniqueness of the Infimum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
$i,j\in S$ are both infima of $A$, then $i=j$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty. If
   > $i,j\in S$ are both infima of $A$, then $i=j$.

items.title: Upper Bound Property of the Supremum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and
suppose that $s=\sup A$ exists in $S$. Then every element of $A$ lies
below $s$:
\[
 (\forall x\in A)(x\leq s).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and
   > suppose that $s=\sup A$ exists in $S$. Then every element of $A$ lies
   > below $s$:
   > \[
   >  (\forall x\in A)(x\leq s).
   > \]

items.title: Lower Bound Property of the Infimum
items.statement:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and
suppose that $i=\inf A$ exists in $S$. Then every element of $A$ lies
above $i$:
\[
 (\forall x\in A)(i\leq x).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and
   > suppose that $i=\inf A$ exists in $S$. Then every element of $A$ lies
   > above $i$:
   > \[
   >  (\forall x\in A)(i\leq x).
   > \]

items.title: Subset Inclusion Preserves Upper Bounds
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq S$ be nonempty subsets of an ordered set
$(S,\leq)$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound
of $A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq S$ be nonempty subsets of an ordered set
   > $(S,\leq)$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound
   > of $A$.

items.title: Subset Inclusion Preserves Lower Bounds
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq S$ be nonempty subsets of an ordered set
$(S,\leq)$. If $\ell$ is a lower bound of $B$, then $\ell$ is a lower
bound of $A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq S$ be nonempty subsets of an ordered set
   > $(S,\leq)$. If $\ell$ is a lower bound of $B$, then $\ell$ is a lower
   > bound of $A$.

items.title: Supremum Is Monotone Under Inclusion
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. If
$A\subseteq B$, then $\sup A\leq\sup B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. If
   > $A\subseteq B$, then $\sup A\leq\sup B$.

items.title: Infimum Is Monotone Under Inclusion
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. If
$A\subseteq B$, then $\inf B\leq\inf A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. If
   > $A\subseteq B$, then $\inf B\leq\inf A$.

items.title: Upper Bound Comparison with the Supremum
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
$s=\sup A$. For $u\in\mathbb{R}$, the number $u$ is an upper bound of
$A$ if and only if $s\leq u$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
   > $s=\sup A$. For $u\in\mathbb{R}$, the number $u$ is an upper bound of
   > $A$ if and only if $s\leq u$.

items.title: Lower Bound Comparison with the Infimum
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$i=\inf A$. For $\ell\in\mathbb{R}$, the number $\ell$ is a lower bound
of $A$ if and only if $\ell\leq i$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
   > $i=\inf A$. For $\ell\in\mathbb{R}$, the number $\ell$ is a lower bound
   > of $A$ if and only if $\ell\leq i$.

items.title: Every Element Lies Above the Infimum
items.statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$i=\inf A$. Then $i\leq x$ for every $x\in A$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
   > $i=\inf A$. Then $i\leq x$ for every $x\in A$.

items.title: Least Upper Bound Property Implies Existence of Suprema
items.statement:
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. By the least
upper bound property of the real numbers, there exists a real number
$s$ such that $s=\sup S$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. By the least
   > upper bound property of the real numbers, there exists a real number
   > $s$ such that $s=\sup S$.

items.title: Supremum Need Not Belong to the Set
items.statement:
There exists a nonempty bounded above set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
\sup A\notin A.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > There exists a nonempty bounded above set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ such that
   > \[
   > \sup A\notin A.
   > \]

items.title: Greatest Lower Bound Property Implies Existence of Infima
items.statement:
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then there
exists a real number $i$ such that $i=\inf S$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then there
   > exists a real number $i$ such that $i=\inf S$.

items.title: Infimum Need Not Belong to the Set
items.statement:
There exists a nonempty bounded below set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
\inf A\notin A.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > There exists a nonempty bounded below set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ such that
   > \[
   > \inf A\notin A.
   > \]

items.title: Order Comparison of Suprema
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. If every
$x\in A$ is below some $y\in B$, then $\sup A\leq\sup B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. If every
   > $x\in A$ is below some $y\in B$, then $\sup A\leq\sup B$.

items.title: Archimedean Property
items.statement: For every real number $x$, there exists a natural number $n$ such that $n>x$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every real number $x$, there exists a natural number $n$ such that $n>x$.

items.title: Archimedean Reciprocal Form
items.statement:
For every real number $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a natural number
$n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
\[
0<\frac{1}{n}<\varepsilon.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every real number $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a natural number
   > $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
   > \[
   > 0<\frac{1}{n}<\varepsilon.
   > \]

items.title: Archimedean Scaling Form
items.statement: For every $x>0$ and every $y\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $nx>y$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $x>0$ and every $y\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $nx>y$.

items.title: Integer Part Lemma
items.statement:
For every real number $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists an integer
$m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
\[
m\le x<m+1.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every real number $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists an integer
   > $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
   > \[
   > m\le x<m+1.
   > \]

items.title: Archimedean Integer Part Lemma
items.statement:
For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
\[
m-1\le x<m.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
   > \[
   > m-1\le x<m.
   > \]

items.title: Integer Ceiling Lemma
items.statement:
For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
\[
x<m\le x+1.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
   > \[
   > x<m\le x+1.
   > \]

items.title: Integer Above Lemma
items.statement:
For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists an integer $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such
that
\[
x<m.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists an integer $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such
   > that
   > \[
   > x<m.
   > \]

items.title: Unit-Length Interval Contains an Integer
items.statement:
If $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\beta-\alpha>1$, then there exists
$m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
\[
\alpha<m<\beta.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\beta-\alpha>1$, then there exists
   > $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
   > \[
   > \alpha<m<\beta.
   > \]

items.title: Rational Translation Preserves Rationality
items.statement:
If $r,q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
\[
r+q\in\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $r,q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
   > \[
   > r+q\in\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Rational Difference Preserves Rationality
items.statement:
If $r,q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
\[
r-q\in\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $r,q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
   > \[
   > r-q\in\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Nonzero Rational Product Preserves Irrationality
items.statement:
If $q\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$ and
$x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, then
\[
qx\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $q\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$ and
   > $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, then
   > \[
   > qx\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Rational Translation Preserves Irrationality
items.statement:
If $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, then
\[
q+x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, then
   > \[
   > q+x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Irrational Minus Irrational Need Not Be Irrational
items.statement:
There exist irrational numbers $x,y\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such
that
\[
x-y\in\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > There exist irrational numbers $x,y\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such
   > that
   > \[
   > x-y\in\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Rational Minus Irrational Is Irrational
items.statement:
If $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, then
\[
q-x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, then
   > \[
   > q-x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Irrational Plus Rational Is Irrational
items.statement:
If $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ and $q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
\[
x+q\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ and $q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
   > \[
   > x+q\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Irrational Minus Rational Is Irrational
items.statement:
If $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ and $q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
\[
x-q\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ and $q\in\mathbb{Q}$, then
   > \[
   > x-q\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.
   > \]

items.title: Density of the Irrationals
items.statement: For every $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, there exists $s\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such that $a<s<b$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, there exists $s\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such that $a<s<b$.

items.title: An Irrational Between Any Two Rationals
items.statement:
If $r,s\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $r<s$, then there exists
$x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such that
\[
r<x<s.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $r,s\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $r<s$, then there exists
   > $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such that
   > \[
   > r<x<s.
   > \]

items.title: A Rational Between Any Two Irrationals
items.statement:
If $x,y\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ and $x<y$, then there exists
$q\in\mathbb{Q}$ such that
\[
x<q<y.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $x,y\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ and $x<y$, then there exists
   > $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ such that
   > \[
   > x<q<y.
   > \]

items.title: Small Irrational Positive Number
items.statement:
For every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists
$\eta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such that
\[
0<\eta<\varepsilon.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists
   > $\eta\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ such that
   > \[
   > 0<\eta<\varepsilon.
   > \]

items.title: No Adjacent Real Numbers
items.statement:
If $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a<b$, then there exists $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
a<c<b.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a<b$, then there exists $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
   > \[
   > a<c<b.
   > \]

items.title: No Immediate Successors in $\mathbb{R}$
items.statement: For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$, there is no least real number greater than $a$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$, there is no least real number greater than $a$.

items.title: No Immediate Predecessors in $\mathbb{R}$
items.statement: For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$, there is no greatest real number less than $a$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$, there is no greatest real number less than $a$.

items.title: Rational and Irrational Points in Every Open Interval
items.statement: Every open interval in $\mathbb{R}$ contains both a rational number and an irrational number.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every open interval in $\mathbb{R}$ contains both a rational number and an irrational number.

items.title: Nested Closed Intervals Have Ordered Endpoints
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of closed intervals such that
\[
 [a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq [a_n,b_n]
\]
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Then
\[
 a_n\le a_{n+1}\le b_{n+1}\le b_n
\]
for every $n\in\mathbb N$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of closed intervals such that
   > \[
   >  [a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq [a_n,b_n]
   > \]
   > for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Then
   > \[
   >  a_n\le a_{n+1}\le b_{n+1}\le b_n
   > \]
   > for every $n\in\mathbb N$.

items.title: Left Endpoints of Nested Intervals Are Increasing
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals.
Then the sequence $(a_n)$ is monotone increasing.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals.
   > Then the sequence $(a_n)$ is monotone increasing.

items.title: Right Endpoints of Nested Intervals Are Decreasing
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals.
Then the sequence $(b_n)$ is monotone decreasing.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals.
   > Then the sequence $(b_n)$ is monotone decreasing.

items.title: Left Endpoints Are Bounded Above by Right Endpoints
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals.
Then for all $m,n\in\mathbb N$,
\[
 a_n\le b_m.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals.
   > Then for all $m,n\in\mathbb N$,
   > \[
   >  a_n\le b_m.
   > \]

items.title: Endpoint Supremum Infimum Inequality
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals. If
\[
 \alpha=\sup\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \beta=\inf\{b_n:n\in\mathbb N\},
\]
then
\[
 \alpha\le \beta.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of closed intervals. If
   > \[
   >  \alpha=\sup\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\}
   >  \quad\text{and}\quad
   >  \beta=\inf\{b_n:n\in\mathbb N\},
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   >  \alpha\le \beta.
   > \]

items.title: Nested Interval Theorem
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of nonempty closed bounded
intervals in $\mathbb R$ such that
\[
 [a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq [a_n,b_n]
\]
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Then
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n]\neq\varnothing.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of nonempty closed bounded
   > intervals in $\mathbb R$ such that
   > \[
   >  [a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq [a_n,b_n]
   > \]
   > for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Then
   > \[
   >  \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n]\neq\varnothing.
   > \]

items.title: Nested Interval Intersection Contains the Endpoint Supremum
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
bounded intervals. If
\[
 \alpha=\sup\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\},
\]
then
\[
 \alpha\in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n].
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
   > bounded intervals. If
   > \[
   >  \alpha=\sup\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\},
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   >  \alpha\in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n].
   > \]

items.title: Nested Interval Intersection Contains the Endpoint Infimum
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
bounded intervals. If
\[
 \beta=\inf\{b_n:n\in\mathbb N\},
\]
then
\[
 \beta\in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n].
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
   > bounded intervals. If
   > \[
   >  \beta=\inf\{b_n:n\in\mathbb N\},
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   >  \beta\in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n].
   > \]

items.title: Nested Intervals with Vanishing Length Have Unique Point
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
bounded intervals. If
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}(b_n-a_n)=0,
\]
then there exists a unique $x\in\mathbb R$ such that
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n]=\{x\}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
   > bounded intervals. If
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}(b_n-a_n)=0,
   > \]
   > then there exists a unique $x\in\mathbb R$ such that
   > \[
   >  \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n]=\{x\}.
   > \]

items.title: Nested Intervals with Vanishing Length Have Equal Endpoint Limits
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
bounded intervals. If
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}(b_n-a_n)=0,
\]
then $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ converge and
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
   > bounded intervals. If
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}(b_n-a_n)=0,
   > \]
   > then $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ converge and
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n.
   > \]

items.title: Unique Point in Nested Intervals Is Endpoint Limit
items.statement:
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
bounded intervals. If
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}(b_n-a_n)=0
\]
and
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n]=\{x\},
\]
then
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=x
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \lim_{n\to\infty}b_n=x.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a nested sequence of nonempty closed
   > bounded intervals. If
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}(b_n-a_n)=0
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   >  \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[a_n,b_n]=\{x\},
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=x
   >  \quad\text{and}\quad
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}b_n=x.
   > \]

items.title: Open Nested Intervals Need Not Have Nonempty Intersection
items.statement:
There exists a nested sequence of nonempty open bounded intervals $(a_n,b_n)$
such that
\[
 (a_{n+1},b_{n+1})\subseteq (a_n,b_n)
\]
for every $n\in\mathbb N$, but
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_n,b_n)=\varnothing.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > There exists a nested sequence of nonempty open bounded intervals $(a_n,b_n)$
   > such that
   > \[
   >  (a_{n+1},b_{n+1})\subseteq (a_n,b_n)
   > \]
   > for every $n\in\mathbb N$, but
   > \[
   >  \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_n,b_n)=\varnothing.
   > \]

items.title: Closedness Is Necessary in the Nested Interval Theorem
items.statement:
The conclusion of the Nested Interval Theorem can fail if the intervals are
not closed.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The conclusion of the Nested Interval Theorem can fail if the intervals are
   > not closed.

items.title: Boundedness Is Necessary in the Nested Interval Theorem
items.statement:
The conclusion of the Nested Interval Theorem can fail for nested nonempty
closed intervals that are not bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The conclusion of the Nested Interval Theorem can fail for nested nonempty
   > closed intervals that are not bounded.

items.title: Order Separation by Supremum
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty sets such that
\[
a\le b
\]
for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.
Then there exists $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
a\le c\le b
\]
for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty sets such that
   > \[
   > a\le b
   > \]
   > for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.
   > Then there exists $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
   > \[
   > a\le c\le b
   > \]
   > for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.

items.title: Dedekind Cut Property
items.statement:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty sets such that
\[
A\cup B=\mathbb{R},\qquad A\cap B=\varnothing,
\]
and
\[
a<b
\]
for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.
Then there exists $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
a\le c\le b
\]
for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty sets such that
   > \[
   > A\cup B=\mathbb{R},\qquad A\cap B=\varnothing,
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > a<b
   > \]
   > for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.
   > Then there exists $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
   > \[
   > a\le c\le b
   > \]
   > for every $a\in A$ and every $b\in B$.

items.title: No Gaps in $\mathbb{R}$
items.statement: The real line has no Dedekind gaps.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The real line has no Dedekind gaps.

items.title: Absolute Value Is Distance to the Origin
items.statement: For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$, $\;|a|=d(a,0)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$, $\;|a|=d(a,0)$.

items.title: Closed Sets Contain Their Limit Points
items.statement: A set $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is closed if and only if it contains every one of its limit points.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A set $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is closed if and only if it contains every one of its limit points.

items.title: Compact Subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ Are Closed and Bounded
items.statement: If $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact, then $K$ is closed and bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact, then $K$ is closed and bounded.

items.title: Closed Bounded Intervals Are Compact
items.statement: Every closed bounded interval $[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every closed bounded interval $[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact.

items.title: Heine--Borel Theorem for $\mathbb{R}$
items.statement: A set $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact if and only if $K$ is closed and bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A set $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact if and only if $K$ is closed and bounded.

items.title: Open Intervals Are Open
items.statement: Every open interval $(a,b)$, every open ray $(a,\infty)$ and $(-\infty,b)$, and $\mathbb{R}$ itself are open sets.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every open interval $(a,b)$, every open ray $(a,\infty)$ and $(-\infty,b)$, and $\mathbb{R}$ itself are open sets.

items.title: Unions and Finite Intersections of Open Sets
items.statement: An arbitrary union of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is open, and a finite intersection of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is open.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > An arbitrary union of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is open, and a finite intersection of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is open.

items.title: Minimum of Positive Numbers Is Positive
items.statement:
If $a>0$ and $b>0$, then
\[
\min\{a,b\}>0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $a>0$ and $b>0$, then
   > \[
   > \min\{a,b\}>0.
   > \]

items.title: Half Epsilon Is Positive
items.statement:
If $\varepsilon>0$, then
\[
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}>0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\varepsilon>0$, then
   > \[
   > \frac{\varepsilon}{2}>0.
   > \]

items.title: Epsilon Splitting
items.statement:
If $\varepsilon>0$, then
\[
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}=\varepsilon.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\varepsilon>0$, then
   > \[
   > \frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}=\varepsilon.
   > \]

items.title: Positive Minimum Bound
items.statement:
If $0<\delta\le a$ and $0<\delta\le b$, then
\[
\delta\le \min\{a,b\}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $0<\delta\le a$ and $0<\delta\le b$, then
   > \[
   > \delta\le \min\{a,b\}.
   > \]

items.title: Choosing a Smaller Positive Number
items.statement:
If $\varepsilon>0$ and $c>0$, then there exists $\delta>0$ such that
\[
0<\delta<\varepsilon
\quad\text{and}\quad
0<\delta<c.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\varepsilon>0$ and $c>0$, then there exists $\delta>0$ such that
   > \[
   > 0<\delta<\varepsilon
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > 0<\delta<c.
   > \]

items.title: The Distance Function Is a Metric
items.statement: The map $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ satisfies, for all $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}$: (i) $d(x,y)\ge 0$ with $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$; (ii) $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$; and (iii) $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Hence $(\mathbb{R},d)$ is a metric space.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The map $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ satisfies, for all $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}$: (i) $d(x,y)\ge 0$ with $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$; (ii) $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$; and (iii) $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Hence $(\mathbb{R},d)$ is a metric space.

items.title: Real Line Structural Order Facts
items.statement:
The real numbers are linearly ordered, form an ordered field, and satisfy the
least upper bound property.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The real numbers are linearly ordered, form an ordered field, and satisfy the
   > least upper bound property.

items.title: Closure Laws for Closed Sets
items.statement: An arbitrary intersection of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed, and a finite union of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > An arbitrary intersection of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed, and a finite union of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed.

items.title: Composition of Injections Is Injective
items.statement:
Let $f:A\to B$ and let $g:B\to C$. If $f$ is injective and $g$ is
injective, then $g\circ f:A\to C$ is injective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f:A\to B$ and let $g:B\to C$. If $f$ is injective and $g$ is
   > injective, then $g\circ f:A\to C$ is injective.

items.title: Composition of Surjections Is Surjective
items.statement:
$\operatorname{Surjective}(f)\wedge\operatorname{Surjective}(g)
\Rightarrow\operatorname{Surjective}(g\circ f)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > $\operatorname{Surjective}(f)\wedge\operatorname{Surjective}(g)
   > \Rightarrow\operatorname{Surjective}(g\circ f)$.

items.title: Composition of Bijections Is Bijective
items.statement:
Let $f:A\to B$ and let $g:B\to C$. If $f$ is bijective and $g$ is
bijective, then $g\circ f:A\to C$ is bijective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f:A\to B$ and let $g:B\to C$. If $f$ is bijective and $g$ is
   > bijective, then $g\circ f:A\to C$ is bijective.

items.title: Inverse of a Bijection Is a Bijection
items.statement: $\operatorname{Bijective}(f)\Rightarrow\operatorname{Bijective}(f^{-1})$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > $\operatorname{Bijective}(f)\Rightarrow\operatorname{Bijective}(f^{-1})$.

items.title: Preimage Distributes over Union and Intersection
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f:A\to B$, $S,T\subseteq B$. Then:
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - $f^{-1}(S\cup T)=f^{-1}(S)\cup f^{-1}(T)$.
   > - $f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)$.
   > - $f^{-1}(S^c)=(f^{-1}(S))^c$.

items.title: Sequential Characterization of Cluster Points
items.statement:
$c\text{ is a cluster point of }A$ if and only if there exists
$(a_n) \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$ with $a_n \to c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > $c\text{ is a cluster point of }A$ if and only if there exists
   > $(a_n) \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$ with $a_n \to c$.

items.title: Elementary Properties of Closures
Closed iff Sequentially Closed
items.statement:
$X\text{ is closed} \iff \forall (a_n)\subseteq X,\;
a_n \to x \Rightarrow x \in X$.

items.title: Every Point of an Interval Is a Cluster Point
items.statement: If $I$ is an interval, then every $x\in I$ is a cluster point of $I$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $I$ is an interval, then every $x\in I$ is a cluster point of $I$.

items.title: Heine--Borel Theorem for $\mathbb{R}$
items.statement:
$X\text{ is closed} \wedge X\text{ is bounded}$
$\iff$ every $(a_n)\subseteq X$ has a subsequence converging to
a limit in $X$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > $X\text{ is closed} \wedge X\text{ is bounded}$
   > $\iff$ every $(a_n)\subseteq X$ has a subsequence converging to
   > a limit in $X$.

items.title: Linearity of \(\Delta\)
items.statement:
For functions \(f,g : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}\) and constants \(a,b \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
\Delta (a f + b g)
=
a\,\Delta f + b\,\Delta g.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For functions \(f,g : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}\) and constants \(a,b \in \mathbb{R}\),
   > \[
   > \Delta (a f + b g)
   > =
   > a\,\Delta f + b\,\Delta g.
   > \]

items.title: Constant rule
items.statement: If \(c\) is a constant function, then \(\Delta c = 0\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(c\) is a constant function, then \(\Delta c = 0\).

items.title: \(\Delta = E - I\)
items.statement:
\[
\Delta = E - I.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > \[
   > \Delta = E - I.
   > \]

items.title: Polynomial detection
items.statement:
Let \(f(n)\) be a sequence generated by a polynomial of degree \(d\). Then
\(\Delta^d f(n)\) is constant, and \(\Delta^{d+1} f(n) = 0\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(f(n)\) be a sequence generated by a polynomial of degree \(d\). Then
   > \(\Delta^d f(n)\) is constant, and \(\Delta^{d+1} f(n) = 0\).

items.title: Constant of integration
items.statement:
If \(F\) is a discrete antiderivative of \(f\), then so is \(F + C\)
for any constant \(C \in \mathbb{R}\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(F\) is a discrete antiderivative of \(f\), then so is \(F + C\)
   > for any constant \(C \in \mathbb{R}\).

items.title: Binomial Theorem
items.statement:
For any integer \(n \ge 0\) and real numbers \(x,y\),
\[
(x+y)^n
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^{\,n-k} y^{\,k},
\]
where the \emph{binomial coefficients} are
\[
\binom{n}{k}
=
\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any integer \(n \ge 0\) and real numbers \(x,y\),
   > \[
   > (x+y)^n
   > =
   > \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^{\,n-k} y^{\,k},
   > \]
   > where the \emph{binomial coefficients} are
   > \[
   > \binom{n}{k}
   > =
   > \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}.
   > \]

items.title: Higher difference formula
items.statement:
For any function \(f\),
\[
\Delta^n f(x)
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{\,n-k}
\binom{n}{k}
f(x+k).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For any function \(f\),
   > \[
   > \Delta^n f(x)
   > =
   > \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^{\,n-k}
   > \binom{n}{k}
   > f(x+k).
   > \]

items.title: Higher differences of \(2^n\)
items.statement:
For all \(k \ge 0\),
\[
\Delta^k\, 2^n = 2^n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all \(k \ge 0\),
   > \[
   > \Delta^k\, 2^n = 2^n.
   > \]

items.title: Discrete IVP
items.statement:
The unique function \(F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfying
\[
F(n+1) = 2\,F(n), \qquad F(0) = 1
\]
is \(F(n) = 2^n\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The unique function \(F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfying
   > \[
   > F(n+1) = 2\,F(n), \qquad F(0) = 1
   > \]
   > is \(F(n) = 2^n\).

items.title: Nonzero Limit is Eventually Nonzero
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\neq 0$.
If $x_n\to L$, then there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\neq 0$
for every $n\ge N$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\neq 0$.
   > If $x_n\to L$, then there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\neq 0$
   > for every $n\ge N$.

items.title: Limit of a Product
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
If $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_ny_n\to LM$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > If $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_ny_n\to LM$.

items.title: Limit of a Reciprocal
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence such that $x_n\neq 0$ for every
$n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\neq 0$. If $x_n\to L$,
then $1/x_n\to 1/L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence such that $x_n\neq 0$ for every
   > $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\neq 0$. If $x_n\to L$,
   > then $1/x_n\to 1/L$.

items.title: Limit of a Quotient
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences such that $y_n\neq 0$ for every
$n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$ with $M\neq 0$. If
$x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_n/y_n\to L/M$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences such that $y_n\neq 0$ for every
   > $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$ with $M\neq 0$. If
   > $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_n/y_n\to L/M$.

items.title: Limit of a Scalar Multiple
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, let $L\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$, then $\alpha x_n\to \alpha L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, let $L\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
   > $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$, then $\alpha x_n\to \alpha L$.

items.title: Limit of a Sum
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
If $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_n+y_n\to L+M$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > If $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_n+y_n\to L+M$.

items.title: Limit of a Square
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
then $x_n^2\to L^2$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
   > then $x_n^2\to L^2$.

items.title: Polynomial Sequence Limit
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, let $L\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
$p\in\mathbb{R}[t]$ be a polynomial. If $x_n\to L$, then
$p(x_n)\to p(L)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, let $L\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
   > $p\in\mathbb{R}[t]$ be a polynomial. If $x_n\to L$, then
   > $p(x_n)\to p(L)$.

items.title: Rational Sequence Limit
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, let $L\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
$p,q\in\mathbb{R}[t]$ be polynomials. Suppose $q(L)\neq 0$ and
$q(x_n)\neq 0$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. If $x_n\to L$, then
\[
\frac{p(x_n)}{q(x_n)}\to \frac{p(L)}{q(L)}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, let $L\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
   > $p,q\in\mathbb{R}[t]$ be polynomials. Suppose $q(L)\neq 0$ and
   > $q(x_n)\neq 0$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$. If $x_n\to L$, then
   > \[
   > \frac{p(x_n)}{q(x_n)}\to \frac{p(L)}{q(L)}.
   > \]

items.title: Monotone Convergence Theorem
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence.
- [label=(\alph*)]
- If $(x_n)$ is increasing and bounded above, then $(x_n)$ converges and
 \[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\sup\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}.
 \]
- If $(x_n)$ is decreasing and bounded below, then $(x_n)$ converges and
 \[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\inf\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}.
 \]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence.
   > - [label=(\alph*)]
   > - If $(x_n)$ is increasing and bounded above, then $(x_n)$ converges and
   >  \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\sup\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}.
   >  \]
   > - If $(x_n)$ is decreasing and bounded below, then $(x_n)$ converges and
   >  \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\inf\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}.
   >  \]

items.title: Newton Approximation of $\sqrt{2}$
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be the Newton sequence for $\sqrt{2}$. Then $(x_n)$ converges
and
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\sqrt{2}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be the Newton sequence for $\sqrt{2}$. Then $(x_n)$ converges
   > and
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\sqrt{2}.
   > \]

items.title: Convergent Sequences Are Cauchy
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ converges, then $(x_n)$ is
Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ converges, then $(x_n)$ is
   > Cauchy.

items.title: Cauchy Sequences Are Bounded
items.statement: Every Cauchy real sequence is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every Cauchy real sequence is bounded.

items.title: Cauchy Sequence with a Convergent Subsequence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence. If a subsequence of $(x_n)$
converges to $L\in\mathbb{R}$, then $(x_n)$ converges to $L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence. If a subsequence of $(x_n)$
   > converges to $L\in\mathbb{R}$, then $(x_n)$ converges to $L$.

items.title: Bounded Monotone Sequence Equivalences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence.
- [label=(\alph*)]
- If $(x_n)$ is increasing, then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
 $(x_n)$ is bounded above.
- If $(x_n)$ is decreasing, then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
 $(x_n)$ is bounded below.
- If $(x_n)$ is monotone, then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
 $(x_n)$ is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence.
   > - [label=(\alph*)]
   > - If $(x_n)$ is increasing, then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
   >  $(x_n)$ is bounded above.
   > - If $(x_n)$ is decreasing, then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
   >  $(x_n)$ is bounded below.
   > - If $(x_n)$ is monotone, then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
   >  $(x_n)$ is bounded.

items.title: Boundedness Passes to Subsequences
items.statement: Every subsequence of a bounded real sequence is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every subsequence of a bounded real sequence is bounded.

items.title: Monotone Subsequence Theorem
items.statement: Every real sequence has a monotone subsequence.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every real sequence has a monotone subsequence.

items.title: Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem for Sequences
items.statement: Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.

items.title: Cauchy Criterion for Real Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
$(x_n)$ is Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Then $(x_n)$ converges if and only if
   > $(x_n)$ is Cauchy.

items.title: Factorial Partial Sums Approximate $e$
items.statement:
Let $(s_n)$ be the factorial partial-sum sequence. Then $(s_n)$ converges
to the Euler number $e$:
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}s_n=e.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(s_n)$ be the factorial partial-sum sequence. Then $(s_n)$ converges
   > to the Euler number $e$:
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}s_n=e.
   > \]

items.title: Uniqueness of Limits
items.statement:
Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. If $x_n \to L$ and $x_n \to K$, then
$L = K$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. If $x_n \to L$ and $x_n \to K$, then
   > $L = K$.

items.title: Limit Preserves Eventual Order
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
Suppose that $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$. If there exists
$N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\le y_n$ for every $n\ge N_0$, then
$L\le M$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > Suppose that $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$. If there exists
   > $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\le y_n$ for every $n\ge N_0$, then
   > $L\le M$.

items.title: Sequence Squeeze Theorem
items.statement:
Let $(a_n)$, $(x_n)$, and $(b_n)$ be real sequences, and let
$L\in\mathbb{R}$. Suppose that $a_n\to L$ and $b_n\to L$. If there
exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $a_n\le x_n\le b_n$ for every
$n\ge N_0$, then $x_n\to L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(a_n)$, $(x_n)$, and $(b_n)$ be real sequences, and let
   > $L\in\mathbb{R}$. Suppose that $a_n\to L$ and $b_n\to L$. If there
   > exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $a_n\le x_n\le b_n$ for every
   > $n\ge N_0$, then $x_n\to L$.

items.title: Compound-Interest Approximation of $e$
items.statement:
Let $(c_n)$ be the compound-interest sequence. Then
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}c_n=e.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(c_n)$ be the compound-interest sequence. Then
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}c_n=e.
   > \]

items.title: Decimal Truncations Converge
items.statement:
Let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $(d_n)$ be the decimal truncation
sequence of $\alpha$. Then
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}d_n=\alpha.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $(d_n)$ be the decimal truncation
   > sequence of $\alpha$. Then
   > \[
   >  \lim_{n\to\infty}d_n=\alpha.
   > \]

items.title: Cauchy Criterion via Tails
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Then $(x_n)$ is Cauchy if and only if
for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that the
$N$-tail has pairwise term distances less than $\varepsilon$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Then $(x_n)$ is Cauchy if and only if
   > for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that the
   > $N$-tail has pairwise term distances less than $\varepsilon$.

items.title: Cauchy Tail Diameter Criterion
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Then $(x_n)$ is Cauchy if and only if
every sufficiently late tail has arbitrarily small pairwise diameter.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Then $(x_n)$ is Cauchy if and only if
   > every sufficiently late tail has arbitrarily small pairwise diameter.

items.title: Cauchy Sequences Have Vanishing Successive Differences
items.statement:
If $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy real sequence, then
\[
 |x_{n+1}-x_n|\to 0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy real sequence, then
   > \[
   >  |x_{n+1}-x_n|\to 0.
   > \]

items.title: Scalar Multiples of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence, and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.
Then $(\alpha x_n)$ is Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence, and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > Then $(\alpha x_n)$ is Cauchy.

items.title: Sums of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. Then $(x_n+y_n)$ is
Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. Then $(x_n+y_n)$ is
   > Cauchy.

items.title: Differences of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. Then $(x_n-y_n)$ is
Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. Then $(x_n-y_n)$ is
   > Cauchy.

items.title: Linear Combinations of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences, and let
$\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $(\alpha x_n+\beta y_n)$ is Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences, and let
   > $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $(\alpha x_n+\beta y_n)$ is Cauchy.

items.title: Products of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. Then $(x_ny_n)$ is
Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. Then $(x_ny_n)$ is
   > Cauchy.

items.title: Reciprocals of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence. If there exist $c>0$ and
$N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $|x_n|\ge c$ for every $n\ge N_0$, then
$(1/x_n)$ is Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence. If there exist $c>0$ and
   > $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $|x_n|\ge c$ for every $n\ge N_0$, then
   > $(1/x_n)$ is Cauchy.

items.title: Quotients of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. If there exist $c>0$
and $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $|y_n|\ge c$ for every $n\ge N_0$,
then $(x_n/y_n)$ is Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be Cauchy real sequences. If there exist $c>0$
   > and $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $|y_n|\ge c$ for every $n\ge N_0$,
   > then $(x_n/y_n)$ is Cauchy.

items.title: Absolute Values of Cauchy Sequences
items.statement: Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence. Then $(|x_n|)$ is Cauchy.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy real sequence. Then $(|x_n|)$ is Cauchy.

items.title: Frequent Properties Yield Subsequences
items.statement:
Let $P(n)$ be a property of indices. If for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ there
exists $n\ge N$ such that $P(n)$ holds, then there exists a strictly
increasing index map $\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that
$P(\sigma(k))$ holds for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $P(n)$ be a property of indices. If for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ there
   > exists $n\ge N$ such that $P(n)$ holds, then there exists a strictly
   > increasing index map $\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that
   > $P(\sigma(k))$ holds for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$.

items.title: Cluster Values Are Subsequential Limits
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $L$ is a
cluster value of $(x_n)$ if and only if $L$ is a subsequential limit of
$(x_n)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $L$ is a
   > cluster value of $(x_n)$ if and only if $L$ is a subsequential limit of
   > $(x_n)$.

items.title: Bounded Sequences Have Cluster Values
items.statement: Every bounded real sequence has at least one cluster value.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every bounded real sequence has at least one cluster value.

items.title: Limsup Is the Largest Subsequential Limit
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let
$S=\limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n$. Then $S$ is a subsequential limit of
$(x_n)$, and every subsequential limit of $(x_n)$ is less than or equal
to $S$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let
   > $S=\limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n$. Then $S$ is a subsequential limit of
   > $(x_n)$, and every subsequential limit of $(x_n)$ is less than or equal
   > to $S$.

items.title: Liminf Is the Smallest Subsequential Limit
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let
$I=\liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n$. Then $I$ is a subsequential limit of
$(x_n)$, and every subsequential limit of $(x_n)$ is greater than or
equal to $I$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let
   > $I=\liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n$. Then $I$ is a subsequential limit of
   > $(x_n)$, and every subsequential limit of $(x_n)$ is greater than or
   > equal to $I$.

items.title: Limsup and Liminf Are Extremal Cluster Values
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. Then
$\limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n$ is the largest cluster value of $(x_n)$, and
$\liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n$ is the smallest cluster value of $(x_n)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. Then
   > $\limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n$ is the largest cluster value of $(x_n)$, and
   > $\liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n$ is the smallest cluster value of $(x_n)$.

items.title: Limit of a Negation
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
then $-x_n\to -L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
   > then $-x_n\to -L$.

items.title: Limit of a Difference
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
If $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_n-y_n\to L-M$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L,M\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > If $x_n\to L$ and $y_n\to M$, then $x_n-y_n\to L-M$.

items.title: Limit of an Absolute Value
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
then $|x_n|\to |L|$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
   > then $|x_n|\to |L|$.

items.title: Positive Limit is Eventually Positive
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L>0$. If $x_n\to L$, then there
exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $0<x_n$ for every $n\ge N$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L>0$. If $x_n\to L$, then there
   > exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $0<x_n$ for every $n\ge N$.

items.title: Limit of a Square Root
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence such that $0\le x_n$ for every
$n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$, then
$0\le L$ and $\sqrt{x_n}\to\sqrt{L}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence such that $0\le x_n$ for every
   > $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$, then
   > $0\le L$ and $\sqrt{x_n}\to\sqrt{L}$.

items.title: Equivalence of Convergence Formulations
items.statement:
Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. The following
statements are equivalent.
- [label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
- $x_n \to L$.
- $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
 \;\bigl(|x_n - L| < \varepsilon\bigr)$.
- $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
 \;\bigl(L - \varepsilon < x_n < L + \varepsilon\bigr)$.
- $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
 \;\bigl(x_n \in V_\varepsilon(L)\bigr)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. The following
   > statements are equivalent.
   > - [label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
   > - $x_n \to L$.
   > - $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
   >  \;\bigl(|x_n - L| < \varepsilon\bigr)$.
   > - $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
   >  \;\bigl(L - \varepsilon < x_n < L + \varepsilon\bigr)$.
   > - $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
   >  \;\bigl(x_n \in V_\varepsilon(L)\bigr)$.

items.title: Strict Limit Separation Gives Eventual Order
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$.
Suppose that $x_n\to A$ and $y_n\to B$. If $A<B$, then there exists
$N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n<y_n$ for every $n\ge N$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > Suppose that $x_n\to A$ and $y_n\to B$. If $A<B$, then there exists
   > $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n<y_n$ for every $n\ge N$.

items.title: Eventual Strict Comparison Preserves Weak Limit Order
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$.
Suppose that $x_n\to A$ and $y_n\to B$.
- [label=(\alph*)]
- If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n<y_n$ for every
 $n\ge N$, then $A\le B$.
- If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n>y_n$ for every
 $n\ge N$, then $A\ge B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > Suppose that $x_n\to A$ and $y_n\to B$.
   > - [label=(\alph*)]
   > - If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n<y_n$ for every
   >  $n\ge N$, then $A\le B$.
   > - If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n>y_n$ for every
   >  $n\ge N$, then $A\ge B$.

items.title: Constant Comparison for Sequence Limits
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$. Suppose
that $x_n\to A$.
- [label=(\alph*)]
- If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\le B$ for every
 $n\ge N$, then $A\le B$.
- If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n<B$ for every
 $n\ge N$, then $A\le B$.
- If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\ge B$ for every
 $n\ge N$, then $A\ge B$.
- If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n>B$ for every
 $n\ge N$, then $A\ge B$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$. Suppose
   > that $x_n\to A$.
   > - [label=(\alph*)]
   > - If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\le B$ for every
   >  $n\ge N$, then $A\le B$.
   > - If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n<B$ for every
   >  $n\ge N$, then $A\le B$.
   > - If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\ge B$ for every
   >  $n\ge N$, then $A\ge B$.
   > - If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n>B$ for every
   >  $n\ge N$, then $A\ge B$.

items.title: Constant Squeeze Theorem
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If there
exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $L\le x_n\le L$ for every
$n\ge N_0$, then $x_n\to L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If there
   > exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $L\le x_n\le L$ for every
   > $n\ge N_0$, then $x_n\to L$.

items.title: Absolute-Value Squeeze Theorem
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(u_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$.
Suppose that $u_n\to 0$. If there exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
$|x_n-L|\le u_n$ for every $n\ge N_0$, then $x_n\to L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(u_n)$ be real sequences, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$.
   > Suppose that $u_n\to 0$. If there exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
   > $|x_n-L|\le u_n$ for every $n\ge N_0$, then $x_n\to L$.

items.title: Constant Sequence Convergence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. If $x_n = c$
for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $(x_n)$ converges to $c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. If $x_n = c$
   > for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $(x_n)$ converges to $c$.

items.title: Zero Sequence is Null
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $x_n = 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
then $(x_n)$ is a null sequence.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $x_n = 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
   > then $(x_n)$ is a null sequence.

items.title: Constant Null Sequence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. If $x_n = c$
for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $(x_n)$ is a null sequence if and only if
$c = 0$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. If $x_n = c$
   > for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $(x_n)$ is a null sequence if and only if
   > $c = 0$.

items.title: Difference from the Limit is Null
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. The sequence
$(x_n)$ converges to $L$ if and only if the sequence $(x_n - L)$ is a null
sequence.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. The sequence
   > $(x_n)$ converges to $L$ if and only if the sequence $(x_n - L)$ is a null
   > sequence.

items.title: Ultimately Constant Sequence Convergence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $x_n = c$ for every $n \ge N_0$, then
$(x_n)$ converges to $c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   > $c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $x_n = c$ for every $n \ge N_0$, then
   > $(x_n)$ converges to $c$.

items.title: Constant Implies Ultimately Constant
items.statement: Every constant real sequence is ultimately constant.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every constant real sequence is ultimately constant.

items.title: Ultimately Zero Sequence is Null
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If there exists $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such
that $x_n = 0$ for every $n \ge N_0$, then $(x_n)$ is a null sequence.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If there exists $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such
   > that $x_n = 0$ for every $n \ge N_0$, then $(x_n)$ is a null sequence.

items.title: Ultimately Constant Null Sequence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Suppose there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$
and $c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $x_n = c$ for every $n \ge N_0$. Then
$(x_n)$ is a null sequence if and only if $c = 0$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. Suppose there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$
   > and $c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $x_n = c$ for every $n \ge N_0$. Then
   > $(x_n)$ is a null sequence if and only if $c = 0$.

items.title: Tail Equality Preserves Convergence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences. If there exists
$N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n = y_n$ for every $n \ge N_0$, then
for every $L \in \mathbb{R}$, $(x_n)$ converges to $L$ if and only if
$(y_n)$ converges to $L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences. If there exists
   > $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n = y_n$ for every $n \ge N_0$, then
   > for every $L \in \mathbb{R}$, $(x_n)$ converges to $L$ if and only if
   > $(y_n)$ converges to $L$.

items.title: Eventually Bounded Above Tail Formulation
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded above if and
only if there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $M \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
$x_n \le M$ for every $n \ge N_0$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded above if and
   > only if there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $M \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
   > $x_n \le M$ for every $n \ge N_0$.

items.title: Eventually Bounded Below Tail Formulation
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded below if and
only if there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
$m \le x_n$ for every $n \ge N_0$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded below if and
   > only if there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
   > $m \le x_n$ for every $n \ge N_0$.

items.title: Eventually Bounded Tail Formulation
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded if and only
if there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $M > 0$ such that $|x_n| \le M$ for
every $n \ge N_0$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded if and only
   > if there exist $N_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $M > 0$ such that $|x_n| \le M$ for
   > every $n \ge N_0$.

items.title: Bounded Sequence If and Only If Bounded Above and Below
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded if and only
if it is both bounded above and bounded below.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. The sequence $(x_n)$ is bounded if and only
   > if it is both bounded above and bounded below.

items.title: Absolute Bound Gives Upper and Lower Bounds
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $K > 0$. If $|x_n| \le K$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $-K \le x_n \le K$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $K > 0$. If $|x_n| \le K$ for every
   > $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $-K \le x_n \le K$ for every
   > $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

items.title: Upper and Lower Bounds Give an Absolute Bound
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If there exist $m,M \in \mathbb{R}$ such
that $m \le x_n \le M$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then there exists
$K > 0$ such that $|x_n| \le K$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If there exist $m,M \in \mathbb{R}$ such
   > that $m \le x_n \le M$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then there exists
   > $K > 0$ such that $|x_n| \le K$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

items.title: Divergence to Infinity Implies Real Divergence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $x_n\to+\infty$ or $x_n\to-\infty$,
then $(x_n)$ is divergent.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $x_n\to+\infty$ or $x_n\to-\infty$,
   > then $(x_n)$ is divergent.

items.title: Subsequence Indices Dominate the Identity
items.statement:
Let $\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ be a strictly increasing index map.
Then
\[
 k\le \sigma(k)
 \qquad
 \text{for every } k\in\mathbb{N}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ be a strictly increasing index map.
   > Then
   > \[
   >  k\le \sigma(k)
   >  \qquad
   >  \text{for every } k\in\mathbb{N}.
   > \]

items.title: Subsequences Preserve Limits
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
then every subsequence of $(x_n)$ converges to $L$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
   > then every subsequence of $(x_n)$ converges to $L$.

items.title: Subsequential Limit of a Convergent Sequence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
then $L$ is the only possible subsequential limit of $(x_n)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$,
   > then $L$ is the only possible subsequential limit of $(x_n)$.

items.title: Divergence by Two Subsequential Limits
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ has two distinct subsequential
limits, then $(x_n)$ does not converge.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ has two distinct subsequential
   > limits, then $(x_n)$ does not converge.

items.title: Two Subsequential Limits Force Divergence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ has two subsequential limits
$L,K\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\ne K$, then $(x_n)$ is divergent.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ has two subsequential limits
   > $L,K\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\ne K$, then $(x_n)$ is divergent.

items.title: Unbounded Above Sequence Has a Positive-Infinity Subsequence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ is not bounded above, then
there exists a subsequence $(x_{\sigma(k)})$ such that
$x_{\sigma(k)}\to+\infty$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ is not bounded above, then
   > there exists a subsequence $(x_{\sigma(k)})$ such that
   > $x_{\sigma(k)}\to+\infty$.

items.title: Unbounded Below Sequence Has a Negative-Infinity Subsequence
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ is not bounded below, then
there exists a subsequence $(x_{\sigma(k)})$ such that
$x_{\sigma(k)}\to-\infty$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence. If $(x_n)$ is not bounded below, then
   > there exists a subsequence $(x_{\sigma(k)})$ such that
   > $x_{\sigma(k)}\to-\infty$.

items.title: Bounded Divergence Produces Two Subsequential Limits
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. If $(x_n)$ is divergent, then
there exist $L,K\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\ne K$ such that $L$ and $K$ are
subsequential limits of $(x_n)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. If $(x_n)$ is divergent, then
   > there exist $L,K\in\mathbb{R}$ with $L\ne K$ such that $L$ and $K$ are
   > subsequential limits of $(x_n)$.

items.title: Tail Suprema Are Decreasing
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let $(s_n)$ be its tail
supremum sequence. Then $(s_n)$ is decreasing.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let $(s_n)$ be its tail
   > supremum sequence. Then $(s_n)$ is decreasing.

items.title: Tail Infima Are Increasing
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let $(i_n)$ be its tail
infimum sequence. Then $(i_n)$ is increasing.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let $(i_n)$ be its tail
   > infimum sequence. Then $(i_n)$ is increasing.

items.title: Liminf Is Below Limsup
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. Then
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n\le \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. Then
   > \[
   >  \liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n\le \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n.
   > \]

items.title: Convergence iff Liminf Equals Limsup
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
$x_n\to L$ if and only if
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n
 =
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
 =
 L.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
   > $x_n\to L$ if and only if
   > \[
   >  \liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n
   >  =
   >  \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
   >  =
   >  L.
   > \]

items.title: Oscillation Criterion via Liminf and Limsup
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. Then
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n
 <
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
\]
if and only if $(x_n)$ has two distinct subsequential limits.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ be a bounded real sequence. Then
   > \[
   >  \liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n
   >  <
   >  \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
   > \]
   > if and only if $(x_n)$ has two distinct subsequential limits.

items.title: Limsup Comparison Under Eventual Order
items.statement:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be bounded real sequences. If there exists
$N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\le y_n$ for every $n\ge N$, then
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
 \le
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}y_n.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be bounded real sequences. If there exists
   > $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n\le y_n$ for every $n\ge N$, then
   > \[
   >  \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
   >  \le
   >  \limsup_{n\to\infty}y_n.
   > \]

items.title: Liminf Comparison Under Eventual Order

items.title: Limsup Squeeze Under Eventual Order
items.statement:
Let $(a_n)$, $(x_n)$, and $(b_n)$ be bounded real sequences. If there
exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
\[
 a_n\le x_n\le b_n
 \qquad\text{for every }n\ge N,
\]
then
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}a_n
 \le
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
 \le
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}b_n.
\]

   >  \le
   >  \limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n
   >  \le
   >  \limsup_{n\to\infty}b_n.
   > \]
