and \(C^{1,1}(I)\) is not contained in \(C^2(I)\). If \(K\) is a compact
interval, then
\[
 C^2(K)\subseteq C^{1,1}(K)\subsetneq C^1(K),
\]
and the first inclusion is strict.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every nondegenerate interval \(I\),
   > \[
   >  C^{1,1}(I)\subsetneq C^1(I),
   > \]
   > and \(C^{1,1}(I)\) is not contained in \(C^2(I)\). If \(K\) is a compact
   > interval, then
   > \[
   >  C^2(K)\subseteq C^{1,1}(K)\subsetneq C^1(K),
   > \]
   > and the first inclusion is strict.

items.title: Bounded Second Derivative Implies \(C^{1,1}\)
items.statement:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval and let \(f\in C^2(I)\). If
\(|f''(x)|\leq M\) for all \(x\in I\), then \(f\in C^{1,1}(I)\), and \(f'\)
is Lipschitz with constant \(M\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval and let \(f\in C^2(I)\). If
   > \(|f''(x)|\leq M\) for all \(x\in I\), then \(f\in C^{1,1}(I)\), and \(f'\)
   > is Lipschitz with constant \(M\).

items.title: Zero Derivative Implies Constant
items.statement:
Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a closed interval, and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If
\[
f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } x \in (a,b),
\]
then $f$ is constant on $I$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a closed interval, and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If
   > \[
   > f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } x \in (a,b),
   > \]
   > then $f$ is constant on $I$.

items.title: Equal Derivatives Imply Difference Is Constant
items.statement:
Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, and let $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If
\[
f'(x) = g'(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in (a,b),
\]
then there exists $C \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x) = g(x) + C$ for all $x \in I$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, and let $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If
   > \[
   > f'(x) = g'(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in (a,b),
   > \]
   > then there exists $C \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x) = g(x) + C$ for all $x \in I$.

items.title: Nonincreasing Iff Nonpositive Derivative
items.statement:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable on $I$. Then $f$ is nonincreasing on $I$ if and only if
\[
f'(x) \leq 0 \qquad \text{for all } x \in I.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable on $I$. Then $f$ is nonincreasing on $I$ if and only if
   > \[
   > f'(x) \leq 0 \qquad \text{for all } x \in I.
   > \]

items.title: Positive Derivative Implies Locally Increasing
items.statement:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in I$, and suppose that $f$ is differentiable at $c$. If $f'(c) > 0$, then there exists $\delta > 0$ such that
\[
f(x) < f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c - \delta < x < c,
\]
and
\[
f(x) > f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c < x < c + \delta.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in I$, and suppose that $f$ is differentiable at $c$. If $f'(c) > 0$, then there exists $\delta > 0$ such that
   > \[
   > f(x) < f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c - \delta < x < c,
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > f(x) > f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c < x < c + \delta.
   > \]

items.title: Negative Derivative Implies Locally Decreasing
items.statement:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in I$, and suppose that $f$ is differentiable at $c$. If $f'(c) < 0$, then there exists $\delta > 0$ such that
\[
f(x) > f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c - \delta < x < c,
\]
and
\[
f(x) < f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c < x < c + \delta.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in I$, and suppose that $f$ is differentiable at $c$. If $f'(c) < 0$, then there exists $\delta > 0$ such that
   > \[
   > f(x) > f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c - \delta < x < c,
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   > f(x) < f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I \text{ with } c < x < c + \delta.
   > \]

items.title: First Derivative Test: Relative Maximum
items.statement:
Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$, and let $c \in (a,b)$. Suppose $f$ is differentiable on $(a,c)$ and $(c,b)$. If there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $(c-\delta,c+\delta) \subseteq I$ and
\[
f'(x) \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta,c),
\qquad
f'(x) \leq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c,c+\delta),
\]
then $f$ has a relative maximum at $c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$, and let $c \in (a,b)$. Suppose $f$ is differentiable on $(a,c)$ and $(c,b)$. If there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $(c-\delta,c+\delta) \subseteq I$ and
   > \[
   > f'(x) \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta,c),
   > \qquad
   > f'(x) \leq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c,c+\delta),
   > \]
   > then $f$ has a relative maximum at $c$.

items.title: First Derivative Test: Relative Minimum
items.statement:
Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$, and let $c \in (a,b)$. Suppose $f$ is differentiable on $(a,c)$ and $(c,b)$. If there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $(c-\delta,c+\delta) \subseteq I$ and
\[
f'(x) \leq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta,c),
\qquad
f'(x) \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c,c+\delta),
\]
then $f$ has a relative minimum at $c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I := [a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$, and let $c \in (a,b)$. Suppose $f$ is differentiable on $(a,c)$ and $(c,b)$. If there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $(c-\delta,c+\delta) \subseteq I$ and
   > \[
   > f'(x) \leq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta,c),
   > \qquad
   > f'(x) \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in (c,c+\delta),
   > \]
   > then $f$ has a relative minimum at $c$.

items.title: Differential and Derivative Agree
items.statement:
Let $f$ be defined on a neighbourhood of $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $f$ is differentiable at $c$ in the ordinary derivative sense if and only if it is differentiable at $c$ in the differential sense. When this holds,
\[
 df_c(h)=f'(c)h.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f$ be defined on a neighbourhood of $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $f$ is differentiable at $c$ in the ordinary derivative sense if and only if it is differentiable at $c$ in the differential sense. When this holds,
   > \[
   >  df_c(h)=f'(c)h.
   > \]

items.title: Uniqueness of the Differential
items.statement:
If $L_1,L_2:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ are linear maps and
\[
 f(c+h)-f(c)=L_1(h)+o(h)=L_2(h)+o(h)
 \qquad\text{as } h\to 0,
\]
then $L_1=L_2$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $L_1,L_2:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ are linear maps and
   > \[
   >  f(c+h)-f(c)=L_1(h)+o(h)=L_2(h)+o(h)
   >  \qquad\text{as } h\to 0,
   > \]
   > then $L_1=L_2$.

items.title: Differential Continuity Criterion
items.statement: If $f$ is differentiable at $c$ in the differential sense, then $f$ is continuous at $c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $f$ is differentiable at $c$ in the differential sense, then $f$ is continuous at $c$.

items.title: Chain Rule for Differentials
items.statement:
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, then
\[
 d(g\circ f)_c=dg_{f(c)}\circ df_c.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, then
   > \[
   >  d(g\circ f)_c=dg_{f(c)}\circ df_c.
   > \]

items.title: Linearity of the Differential
items.statement:
If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $c$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, then
\[
 d(\alpha f+\beta g)_c=\alpha\,df_c+\beta\,dg_c.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $c$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, then
   > \[
   >  d(\alpha f+\beta g)_c=\alpha\,df_c+\beta\,dg_c.
   > \]

items.title: Taylor's Theorem with Lagrange Remainder
items.statement:
Let $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let
$f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$. Suppose that $f,f',\ldots,f^{(n)}$ are continuous
on $[a,b]$ and that $f^{(n+1)}$ exists on $(a,b)$. Then, for every
$x\in(a,b)$, there exists $c$ strictly between $a$ and $x$ such that
\[
 f(x)
 =
 \sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k
 +
 \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let
   > $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$. Suppose that $f,f',\ldots,f^{(n)}$ are continuous
   > on $[a,b]$ and that $f^{(n+1)}$ exists on $(a,b)$. Then, for every
   > $x\in(a,b)$, there exists $c$ strictly between $a$ and $x$ such that
   > \[
   >  f(x)
   >  =
   >  \sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k
   >  +
   >  \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}.
   > \]

items.title: Taylor Expansion with Peano Remainder
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $a\in I$, let
$n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ have derivatives up to order
$n$ in a neighbourhood of $a$. If $f^{(n)}$ is continuous at $a$, then
\[
 f(x)
 =
 \sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k
 +
 o\bigl((x-a)^n\bigr)
 \qquad\text{as }x\to a.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $I\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $a\in I$, let
   > $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ have derivatives up to order
   > $n$ in a neighbourhood of $a$. If $f^{(n)}$ is continuous at $a$, then
   > \[
   >  f(x)
   >  =
   >  \sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k
   >  +
   >  o\bigl((x-a)^n\bigr)
   >  \qquad\text{as }x\to a.
   > \]

items.title: First-Order Peano Remainder
items.statement:
Let $f$ be differentiable at $c$. Then, as $h\to 0$,
\[
 f(c+h)=f(c)+f'(c)h+o(h).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $f$ be differentiable at $c$. Then, as $h\to 0$,
   > \[
   >  f(c+h)=f(c)+f'(c)h+o(h).
   > \]

items.title: The Flat Function: Smooth but Not Analytic
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by
   > \[
   >  f(x)=
   >  \begin{cases}
   >  e^{-1/x^2}, & x\neq 0,\\
   >  0, & x=0.
   >  \end{cases}
   > \]
   > Then:
   > - \(f\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})\);
   > - \(f^{(n)}(0)=0\) for every \(n\geq 0\);
   > - the Maclaurin series of \(f\) is identically \(0\), so \(f\notin C^\omega\) on any neighbourhood of \(0\).
   > In particular, \(C^\infty(\mathbb{R})\setminus C^\omega(\mathbb{R})\neq\varnothing\).

items.title: Cauchy Integral of a Constant
items.statement: If \(f(x)=c\) on \([a,b]\), then \(\int_a^b c\,dx=c(b-a)\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f(x)=c\) on \([a,b]\), then \(\int_a^b c\,dx=c(b-a)\).

items.title: Linearity of the Cauchy Integral
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are Cauchy-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
\[
 \int_a^b(\alpha f+\beta g)\,dx
 =
 \alpha\int_a^b f\,dx+\beta\int_a^b g\,dx.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(g\) are Cauchy-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b(\alpha f+\beta g)\,dx
   >  =
   >  \alpha\int_a^b f\,dx+\beta\int_a^b g\,dx.
   > \]

items.title: Monotonicity of the Cauchy Integral
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are Cauchy-integrable on \([a,b]\) and \(f(x)\le g(x)\)
for every \(x\in[a,b]\), then
\[
 \int_a^b f\,dx\le \int_a^b g\,dx .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(g\) are Cauchy-integrable on \([a,b]\) and \(f(x)\le g(x)\)
   > for every \(x\in[a,b]\), then
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,dx\le \int_a^b g\,dx .
   > \]

items.title: Bounds for the Cauchy Integral
items.statement:
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), \(m=\min_{[a,b]}f\), and
\(M=\max_{[a,b]}f\), then
\[
 m(b-a)\le \int_a^b f\,dx\le M(b-a).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), \(m=\min_{[a,b]}f\), and
   > \(M=\max_{[a,b]}f\), then
   > \[
   >  m(b-a)\le \int_a^b f\,dx\le M(b-a).
   > \]

items.title: Triangle Inequality for the Cauchy Integral
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(|f|\) are Cauchy-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
\[
 \left|\int_a^b f\,dx\right|\le \int_a^b |f|\,dx .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(|f|\) are Cauchy-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
   > \[
   >  \left|\int_a^b f\,dx\right|\le \int_a^b |f|\,dx .
   > \]

items.title: Continuous Functions Are Cauchy-Integrable
items.statement: Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Cauchy-integrable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Cauchy-integrable.

items.title: Tag Independence for Continuous Functions
items.statement:
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), then every choice of tags gives the same
limit as the left-endpoint sums as \(\|P\|\to 0\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), then every choice of tags gives the same
   > limit as the left-endpoint sums as \(\|P\|\to 0\).

items.title: Darboux Sums Under Refinement
items.statement:
If \(P'\) refines \(P\), then
\[
 L(f,P)\le L(f,P')\le U(f,P')\le U(f,P).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(P'\) refines \(P\), then
   > \[
   >  L(f,P)\le L(f,P')\le U(f,P')\le U(f,P).
   > \]

items.title: Darboux Criterion
items.statement:
A bounded function \(f\) is Darboux-integrable if and only if for every
\(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a partition \(P\) such that
\[
 U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A bounded function \(f\) is Darboux-integrable if and only if for every
   > \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a partition \(P\) such that
   > \[
   >  U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon.
   > \]

items.title: Equivalence of Riemann and Darboux Integrability
items.statement:
For bounded functions on \([a,b]\), Riemann integrability and Darboux
integrability are equivalent, and the integral values agree.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For bounded functions on \([a,b]\), Riemann integrability and Darboux
   > integrability are equivalent, and the integral values agree.

items.title: Continuous Functions Are Darboux-Integrable
items.statement: Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Darboux-integrable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Darboux-integrable.

items.title: Monotone Functions Are Darboux-Integrable
items.statement: Every monotone function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Darboux-integrable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every monotone function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Darboux-integrable.

items.title: Bounded Functions with Finitely Many Discontinuities Are Darboux-Integrable
items.statement:
If \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is bounded and has only finitely many
discontinuities, then \(f\) is Darboux-integrable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is bounded and has only finitely many
   > discontinuities, then \(f\) is Darboux-integrable.

items.title: Sums and Scalar Multiples of Darboux-Integrable Functions
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
\(\alpha f+\beta g\) is Darboux-integrable for all
\(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(g\) are Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
   > \(\alpha f+\beta g\) is Darboux-integrable for all
   > \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\).

items.title: Products of Darboux-Integrable Functions
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(fg\) is
Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(g\) are Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(fg\) is
   > Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\).

items.title: Absolute Values of Darboux-Integrable Functions
items.statement:
If \(f\) is Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(|f|\) is
Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) is Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(|f|\) is
   > Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\).

items.title: Continuous Images of Darboux-Integrable Functions
items.statement:
If \(f\) is Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), \(\varphi\) is continuous on an

interval containing \(f([a,b])\), and \(f\) is bounded, then
\(\varphi\circ f\) is Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) is Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\), \(\varphi\) is continuous on an
   >
   > interval containing \(f([a,b])\), and \(f\) is bounded, then
   > \(\varphi\circ f\) is Darboux-integrable on \([a,b]\).

items.title: Cousin's Lemma
items.statement:
For every gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\), there exists a \(\delta\)-fine tagged
partition of \([a,b]\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\), there exists a \(\delta\)-fine tagged
   > partition of \([a,b]\).

items.title: Riemann Integrable Implies Henstock--Kurzweil Integrable
items.statement:
If \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(f\) is
Henstock--Kurzweil integrable on \([a,b]\), and the two integrals have the
same value.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(f\) is
   > Henstock--Kurzweil integrable on \([a,b]\), and the two integrals have the
   > same value.

items.title: Straddle Lemma
items.statement:
If \(F\) is differentiable at \(\xi\) with \(F'(\xi)=f(\xi)\), then for every
\(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta(\xi)>0\) such that whenever
\(u\le \xi\le v\), \(u,v\in(\xi-\delta(\xi),\xi+\delta(\xi))\),
\[
 |F(v)-F(u)-f(\xi)(v-u)|\le \varepsilon(v-u).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(F\) is differentiable at \(\xi\) with \(F'(\xi)=f(\xi)\), then for every
   > \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta(\xi)>0\) such that whenever
   > \(u\le \xi\le v\), \(u,v\in(\xi-\delta(\xi),\xi+\delta(\xi))\),
   > \[
   >  |F(v)-F(u)-f(\xi)(v-u)|\le \varepsilon(v-u).
   > \]

items.title: Fundamental Theorem for the Henstock--Kurzweil Integral
items.statement:
If \(F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at every point and \(F'=f\), then
\(f\) is Henstock--Kurzweil integrable and
\[
 (\mathrm{HK})\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at every point and \(F'=f\), then
   > \(f\) is Henstock--Kurzweil integrable and
   > \[
   >  (\mathrm{HK})\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a).
   > \]

items.title: Continuous Functions Are Riemann-Integrable
items.statement: Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Riemann-integrable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Riemann-integrable.

items.title: Continuous Functions Are Henstock--Kurzweil Integrable
items.statement:
Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Henstock--Kurzweil
integrable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every continuous function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Henstock--Kurzweil
   > integrable.

items.title: Riemann Integrable Implies McShane Integrable Implies Henstock--Kurzweil Integrable
items.statement:
On a compact interval,
\[
 \mathcal R[a,b]\subseteq \mathcal M[a,b]\subseteq \mathcal{HK}[a,b],
\]
and the integral values agree whenever a function belongs to the smaller
class.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > On a compact interval,
   > \[
   >  \mathcal R[a,b]\subseteq \mathcal M[a,b]\subseteq \mathcal{HK}[a,b],
   > \]
   > and the integral values agree whenever a function belongs to the smaller
   > class.

items.title: Lebesgue Criterion for Riemann Integrability
items.statement:
A bounded function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Riemann-integrable if and only
if its discontinuity set
\[
 D=\{x\in[a,b]:\omega_f(x)>0\}
\]
has measure zero.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A bounded function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is Riemann-integrable if and only
   > if its discontinuity set
   > \[
   >  D=\{x\in[a,b]:\omega_f(x)>0\}
   > \]
   > has measure zero.

items.title: McShane Integrability Equals Lebesgue Integrability
items.statement:
For real-valued functions on a compact interval,
\[
 \mathcal{McShane}[a,b]=\mathcal L[a,b],
\]
and the McShane and Lebesgue integral values agree.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For real-valued functions on a compact interval,
   > \[
   >  \mathcal{McShane}[a,b]=\mathcal L[a,b],
   > \]
   > and the McShane and Lebesgue integral values agree.

items.title: Common Refinement of Two Partitions
items.statement:
Any two partitions \(P\) and \(P'\) of \([a,b]\) have a common refinement:
order the finite set \(P\cup P'\) increasingly.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Any two partitions \(P\) and \(P'\) of \([a,b]\) have a common refinement:
   > order the finite set \(P\cup P'\) increasingly.

items.title: Linearity of the Riemann Integral
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
\[
 \int_a^b(\alpha f+\beta g)\,dx
 =
 \alpha\int_a^b f\,dx+\beta\int_a^b g\,dx .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(g\) are Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b(\alpha f+\beta g)\,dx
   >  =
   >  \alpha\int_a^b f\,dx+\beta\int_a^b g\,dx .
   > \]

items.title: Monotonicity of the Riemann Integral
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\) and \(f(x)\le g(x)\)
for every \(x\in[a,b]\), then
\[
 \int_a^b f\,dx\le \int_a^b g\,dx .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(g\) are Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\) and \(f(x)\le g(x)\)
   > for every \(x\in[a,b]\), then
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,dx\le \int_a^b g\,dx .
   > \]

items.title: Triangle Inequality for the Riemann Integral
items.statement:
If \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(|f|\) is
Riemann-integrable and
\[
 \left|\int_a^b f\,dx\right|\le \int_a^b |f|\,dx .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then \(|f|\) is
   > Riemann-integrable and
   > \[
   >  \left|\int_a^b f\,dx\right|\le \int_a^b |f|\,dx .
   > \]

items.title: Interval Additivity for the Riemann Integral
items.statement:
If \(c\in[a,b]\), then \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\) if and only if
it is Riemann-integrable on \([a,c]\) and \([c,b]\), and in that case
\[
 \int_a^b f\,dx=\int_a^c f\,dx+\int_c^b f\,dx .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(c\in[a,b]\), then \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\) if and only if
   > it is Riemann-integrable on \([a,c]\) and \([c,b]\), and in that case
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,dx=\int_a^c f\,dx+\int_c^b f\,dx .
   > \]

items.title: Cauchy Criterion for Riemann Integrability
items.statement:
A bounded function is Riemann-integrable if and only if for every
\(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that any two tagged partitions
\((P,\xi)\) and \((Q,\eta)\) with \(\|P\|,\|Q\|<\delta\) have
\[
 |S(f,P,\xi)-S(f,Q,\eta)|<\varepsilon.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A bounded function is Riemann-integrable if and only if for every
   > \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that any two tagged partitions
   > \((P,\xi)\) and \((Q,\eta)\) with \(\|P\|,\|Q\|<\delta\) have
   > \[
   >  |S(f,P,\xi)-S(f,Q,\eta)|<\varepsilon.
   > \]

items.title: Monotone Functions Have Bounded Variation
items.statement: If \(\alpha\) is monotone on \([a,b]\), then \(\alpha\) has bounded variation.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(\alpha\) is monotone on \([a,b]\), then \(\alpha\) has bounded variation.

items.title: Continuous Integrand and BV Integrator
items.statement:
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(\alpha\) has bounded variation, then
\(\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\) exists.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(\alpha\) has bounded variation, then
   > \(\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\) exists.

items.title: Bilinearity of the Riemann--Stieltjes Integral
items.statement:
Whenever the displayed integrals exist,
\[
 \int_a^b (\lambda f+\mu g)\,d\alpha
 =
 \lambda\int_a^b f\,d\alpha+\mu\int_a^b g\,d\alpha
\]
an
d
\[
 \int_a^b f\,d(\lambda\alpha+\mu\beta)
 =
 \lambda\int_a^b f\,d\alpha+\mu\int_a^b f\,d\beta .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Whenever the displayed integrals exist,
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b (\lambda f+\mu g)\,d\alpha
   >  =
   >  \lambda\int_a^b f\,d\alpha+\mu\int_a^b g\,d\alpha
   > \]
   > an
   > d
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,d(\lambda\alpha+\mu\beta)
   >  =
   >  \lambda\int_a^b f\,d\alpha+\mu\int_a^b f\,d\beta .
   > \]

items.title: Interval Additivity for the Riemann--Stieltjes Integral
items.statement:
If \(c\in[a,b]\) and the relevant Riemann--Stieltjes integrals exist, then
\[
 \int_a^b f\,d\alpha
 =
 \int_a^c f\,d\alpha+\int_c^b f\,d\alpha .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(c\in[a,b]\) and the relevant Riemann--Stieltjes integrals exist, then
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,d\alpha
   >  =
   >  \int_a^c f\,d\alpha+\int_c^b f\,d\alpha .
   > \]

items.title: Riemann--Stieltjes Integration by Parts
items.statement:
If \(f\) and \(\alpha\) are such that one of
\(\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\) and \(\int_a^b \alpha\,df\) exists, then the other
exists under the same Riemann--Stieltjes convention, and
\[
 \int_a^b f\,d\alpha+\int_a^b \alpha\,df
 =
 f(b)\alpha(b)-f(a)\alpha(a).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(f\) and \(\alpha\) are such that one of
   > \(\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\) and \(\int_a^b \alpha\,df\) exists, then the other
   > exists under the same Riemann--Stieltjes convention, and
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,d\alpha+\int_a^b \alpha\,df
   >  =
   >  f(b)\alpha(b)-f(a)\alpha(a).
   > \]

items.title: Reduction to Riemann Integration for a \(C^1\) Integrator
items.statement:
If \(\alpha\in C^1([a,b])\) and \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
\[
 \int_a^b f\,d\alpha=\int_a^b f(x)\alpha'(x)\,dx .
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(\alpha\in C^1([a,b])\) and \(f\) is Riemann-integrable on \([a,b]\), then
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,d\alpha=\int_a^b f(x)\alpha'(x)\,dx .
   > \]

items.title: Step Integrators Give Finite Sums
items.statement:
If \(\alpha\) is constant except for finitely many jumps at points \(c_k\) and
\(f\) is continuous at each \(c_k\), then
\[
 \int_a^b f\,d\alpha=\sum_k f(c_k)\,\Delta\alpha(c_k).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If \(\alpha\) is constant except for finitely many jumps at points \(c_k\) and
   > \(f\) is continuous at each \(c_k\), then
   > \[
   >  \int_a^b f\,d\alpha=\sum_k f(c_k)\,\Delta\alpha(c_k).
   > \]

items.title: Order Is Translation Invariant
items.statement:
In an ordered field, if
\[
a<b,
\]
then for every $c$,
\[
a+c<b+c.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, if
   > \[
   > a<b,
   > \]
   > then for every $c$,
   > \[
   > a+c<b+c.
   > \]

items.title: Order Is Preserved by Positive Multiplication
items.statement:
In an ordered field, if
\[
a<b
\quad\text{and}\quad
c>0,
\]
then
\[
ac<bc.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, if
   > \[
   > a<b
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > c>0,
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   > ac<bc.
   > \]

items.title: Order Is Reversed by Negative Multiplication
items.statement:
In an ordered field, if
\[
a<b
\quad\text{and}\quad
c<0,
\]
then
\[
bc<ac.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, if
   > \[
   > a<b
   > \quad\text{and}\quad
   > c<0,
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   > bc<ac.
   > \]

items.title: Positive Elements Have Positive Reciprocals
items.statement:
In an ordered field, if
\[
a>0,
\]
then
\[
a^{-1}>0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, if
   > \[
   > a>0,
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   > a^{-1}>0.
   > \]

items.title: Negative Elements Have Negative Reciprocals
items.statement:
In an ordered field, if
\[
a<0,
\]
then
\[
a^{-1}<0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, if
   > \[
   > a<0,
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   > a^{-1}<0.
   > \]

items.title: Squares Are Nonnegative
items.statement:
In an ordered field, for every $x$,
\[
x^2\ge 0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, for every $x$,
   > \[
   > x^2\ge 0.
   > \]

items.title: One Is Positive
items.statement:
In an ordered field,
\[
1>0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field,
   > \[
   > 1>0.
   > \]

items.title: No Ordered Field Has Square Root of Negative One
items.statement:
In an ordered field, there is no $x$ such that
\[
x^2=-1.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, there is no $x$ such that
   > \[
   > x^2=-1.
   > \]

items.title: Product Sign Laws in an Ordered Field
items.statement:
In an ordered field, the usual product sign laws hold:
\[
(+)(+)=(+),\qquad (-)(-)=(+),\qquad (+)(-)=(-),\qquad (-)(+) = (-).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, the usual product sign laws hold:
   > \[
   > (+)(+)=(+),\qquad (-)(-)=(+),\qquad (+)(-)=(-),\qquad (-)(+) = (-).
   > \]

items.title: Division Order Laws in an Ordered Field
items.statement:
In an ordered field, division by a positive element preserves order and
division by a negative element reverses order.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an ordered field, division by a positive element preserves order and
   > division by a negative element reverses order.

items.title: Key Local Ball Lemma
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(y\in B_d(x;r)\), then
\[
 B_d(y;r-d(x,y))\subseteq B_d(x;r).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(y\in B_d(x;r)\), then
   > \[
   >  B_d(y;r-d(x,y))\subseteq B_d(x;r).
   > \]

items.title: Ball Nesting
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x\in X\), and let \(0<r\leq s\).
Then
\[
 B_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(x;s).
\]
If \(r<s\), then also
\[
 \overline{B}_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(x;s).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x\in X\), and let \(0<r\leq s\).
   > Then
   > \[
   >  B_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(x;s).
   > \]
   > If \(r<s\), then also
   > \[
   >  \overline{B}_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(x;s).
   > \]

items.title: Ball Containment by Center Distance
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x,y\in X\), and let \(r,s>0\).

If
\[
 d(x,y)+r\leq s,
\]
then
\[
 B_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(y;s).
\]
If
\[
 d(x,y)+r<s,
\]
then
\[
 \overline{B}_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(y;s).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x,y\in X\), and let \(r,s>0\).
   >
   > If
   > \[
   >  d(x,y)+r\leq s,
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   >  B_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(y;s).
   > \]
   > If
   > \[
   >  d(x,y)+r<s,
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   >  \overline{B}_d(x;r)\subseteq B_d(y;s).
   > \]

items.title: Intersecting Balls Imply Center-Distance Bound
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x,y\in X\), and let \(r,s>0\). If
\[
 B_d(x;r)\cap B_d(y;s)\neq\varnothing,
\]
then
\[
 d(x,y)<r+s.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x,y\in X\), and let \(r,s>0\). If
   > \[
   >  B_d(x;r)\cap B_d(y;s)\neq\varnothing,
   > \]
   > then
   > \[
   >  d(x,y)<r+s.
   > \]

items.title: Closed Balls Contain Open Balls
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x
\in X\) and every \(r>0\),
\[
 B_d(x;r)\subseteq \overline{B}_d(x;r).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x
   > \in X\) and every \(r>0\),
   > \[
   >  B_d(x;r)\subseteq \overline{B}_d(x;r).
   > \]

items.title: Distance to a Union
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x\in X\), and let \(A,B\subseteq X\)
be nonempty. Then
\[
 d(x,A\cup B)=\min\{d(x,A),d(x,B)\}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x\in X\), and let \(A,B\subseteq X\)
   > be nonempty. Then
   > \[
   >  d(x,A\cup B)=\min\{d(x,A),d(x,B)\}.
   > \]

items.title: Distance to an Intersection Bound
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x\in X\), and let
\(A,B\subseteq X\) have nonempty intersection. Then
\[
 d(x,A\cap B)\geq \max\{d(x,A),d(x,B)\}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(x\in X\), and let
   > \(A,B\subseteq X\) have nonempty intersection. Then
   > \[
   >  d(x,A\cap B)\geq \max\{d(x,A),d(x,B)\}.
   > \]

items.title: Equivalent Boundedness Criterion
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(A\subseteq X\). Then \(A\) is
bounded if and only if there exist \(x\in X\) and \(R>0\) such that
\[
 d(x,a)<R
\]
for every \(a\in A\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(A\subseteq X\). Then \(A\) is
   > bounded if and only if there exist \(x\in X\) and \(R>0\) such that
   > \[
   >  d(x,a)<R
   > \]
   > for every \(a\in A\).

items.title: Center Independence
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(A\subseteq X\) and there exist
\(x\in X\) and \(R>0\) such that \(d(x,a)\leq R\) for every \(a\in A\), then
for every \(y\in X\),
\[
 d(y,a)\leq R+d(x,y)
\]
for every \(a\in A\). Thus boundedness does not depend on the chosen center.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(A\subseteq X\) and there exist
   > \(x\in X\) and \(R>0\) such that \(d(x,a)\leq R\) for every \(a\in A\), then
   > for every \(y\in X\),
   > \[
   >  d(y,a)\leq R+d(x,y)
   > \]
   > for every \(a\in A\). Thus boundedness does not depend on the chosen center.

items.title: Subsets of Bounded Sets Are Bounded
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(A\subseteq B\subseteq X\) and \(B\) is
bounded, then \(A\) is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(A\subseteq B\subseteq X\) and \(B\) is
   > bounded, then \(A\) is bounded.

items.title: Finite Sets Are Bounded
items.statement: Every finite subset of a metric space is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every finite subset of a metric space is bounded.

items.title: Finite Unions of Bounded Sets Are Bounded
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), and let
\(A_1,\ldots,A_n\subseteq X\). If \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) are bounded, then
\[
 \bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k
\]
is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), and let
   > \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\subseteq X\). If \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) are bounded, then
   > \[
   >  \bigcup_{k=1}^n A_k
   > \]
   > is bounded.

items.title: Boundedness via Diameter
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(A\subseteq X\) be nonempty. Then
\(A\) is bounded if and only if there exists \(C>0\) such that
\[
 d(a,b)\leq C
\]
for all \(a,b\in A\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(A\subseteq X\) be nonempty. Then
   > \(A\) is bounded if and only if there exists \(C>0\) such that
   > \[
   >  d(a,b)\leq C
   > \]
   > for all \(a,b\in A\).

items.title: Closure of a Bounded Set Is Bounded
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(A\subseteq X\) is bounded, then
\(\operatorname{cl}(A)\) is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. If \(A\subseteq X\) is bounded, then
   > \(\operatorname{cl}(A)\) is bounded.

items.title: Compact Sets Are Bounded
items.statement: Every compact subset of a metric space is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every compact subset of a metric space is bounded.

items.title: Totally Bounded Sets Are Bounded
items.statement: Every totally bounded subset of a metric space is bounded.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every totally bounded subset of a metric space is bounded.

items.title: Metrics are Pseudo-Metrics
items.statement:
Every metric on a nonempty set \(X\) is a pseudo-metric on \(X\).
The converse is false: there exist pseudo-metrics that are not metrics.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every metric on a nonempty set \(X\) is a pseudo-metric on \(X\).
   > The converse is false: there exist pseudo-metrics that are not metrics.

items.title: Closed Sets Contain Their Limit Points
items.statement:
Let \(X\) be a metric space and let \(E\subseteq X\). Then \(E\) is closed if
and only if \(E'\subseteq E\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(X\) be a metric space and let \(E\subseteq X\). Then \(E\) is closed if
   > and only if \(E'\subseteq E\).

items.title: Sequential Characterization of Limit Points
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(E\subseteq X\), and let \(x\in X\).
Then \(x\in E'\) if and only if there exists a sequence of distinct terms in
\(E\) that converges to \(x\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(E\subseteq X\), and let \(x\in X\).
   > Then \(x\in E'\) if and only if there exists a sequence of distinct terms in
   > \(E\) that converges to \(x\).

items.title: Neighborhood Characterization of Limit Points
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(E\subseteq X\), and let \(x\in X\).
Then \(x\in E'\) if and only if every neighborhood of \(x\) contains
infinitely many points of \(E\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(E\subseteq X\), and let \(x\in X\).
   > Then \(x\in E'\) if and only if every neighborhood of \(x\) contains
   > infinitely many points of \(E\).

items.title: Cauchy--Schwarz Inequality
items.statement:
For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
 |x\cdot y|\leq |x|\,|y|.
\]
Equality holds if and only if \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly dependent.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
   > \[
   >  |x\cdot y|\leq |x|\,|y|.
   > \]
   > Equality holds if and only if \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly dependent.

items.title: Minkowski's Inequality
items.statement:
For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
 |x+y|\leq |x|+|y|.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
   > \[
   >  |x+y|\leq |x|+|y|.
   > \]

items.title: Euclidean Metric
items.statement:
For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
 d_2(x,y):=\sqrt{|x_1-y_1|^2+\cdots+|x_n-y_n|^2}.
\]
Then \((\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)\) is a metric space.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define
   > \[
   >  d_2(x,y):=\sqrt{|x_1-y_1|^2+\cdots+|x_n-y_n|^2}.
   > \]
   > Then \((\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)\) is a metric space.

items.title: Bolzano--Weierstrass in \(\mathbb{R}^m\)
items.statement:
Every bounded sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) contains a subsequence that
converges in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every bounded sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) contains a subsequence that
   > converges in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).

items.title: Bolzano--Weierstrass for Bounded Infinite Subsets
items.statement:
Every bounded infinite subset of \(\mathbb{R}^m\) has a limit point in
\(\mathbb{R}^m\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every bounded infinite subset of \(\mathbb{R}^m\) has a limit point in
   > \(\mathbb{R}^m\).

items.title: The Derived Set is Closed
items.statement: The set of limit points of any set is closed.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The set of limit points of any set is closed.

items.title: A Norm Induces a Metric
items.statement:
Let \(V\) be a real vector space and let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(V\).
Define
\[
 d_{\|\cdot\|}:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},
 \qquad
 d_{\|\cdot\|}(x,y):=\|x-y\|.
\]
Then \(d_{\|\cdot\|}\) is a metric on \(V\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(V\) be a real vector space and let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(V\).
   > Define
   > \[
   >  d_{\|\cdot\|}:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},
   >  \qquad
   >  d_{\|\cdot\|}(x,y):=\|x-y\|.
   > \]
   > Then \(d_{\|\cdot\|}\) is a metric on \(V\).

items.title: The Discrete Distance is a Metric
items.statement:
For every nonempty set \(X\), the discrete distance
\(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\) is a metric on \(X\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every nonempty set \(X\), the discrete distance
   > \(d_{\mathrm{disc}}\) is a metric on \(X\).

items.title: The Real-Line Euclidean Distance is a Metric
items.statement: The function \(d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y)=|x-y|\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The function \(d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y)=|x-y|\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}\).

items.title: The Euclidean Distance on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a Metric
items.statement: The function \(d_2\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The function \(d_2\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

items.title: Taxicab Metric
items.statement: The function \(d_1\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The function \(d_1\) is a metric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

items.title: \(d_p\) is a Metric
items.statement:
For every \(1\leq p<\infty\), the function \(d_p\) is a metric on
\(\mathbb{R}^n\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every \(1\leq p<\infty\), the function \(d_p\) is a metric on
   > \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

items.title: The Complex Plane is a Metric Space
items.statement: The pair \((\mathbb{C},d_{\mathbb{C}})\) is a metric space.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The pair \((\mathbb{C},d_{\mathbb{C}})\) is a metric space.

items.title: The Supremum Distance on Bounded Sequences is a Metric
items.statement: The function \(d_\infty\) is a metric on \(\ell^\infty(\mathbb{R})\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The function \(d_\infty\) is a metric on \(\ell^\infty(\mathbb{R})\).

items.title: Point Functions Identify Points
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. The map
\[
 X\to\delta(X),
 \qquad
 z\mapsto\delta_z
\]
is a bijection.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. The map
   > \[
   >  X\to\delta(X),
   >  \qquad
   >  z\mapsto\delta_z
   > \]
   > is a bijection.

items.title: Point Function Inequalities
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a nonempty metric space and let \(z\in X\). Then, for all
\(a,b\in X\),
\[
 \delta_z(b)-\delta_z(a)\leq d(a,b)\leq \delta_z(b)+\delta_z(a),
\]
and
\[
 \delta_z(z)=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a nonempty metric space and let \(z\in X\). Then, for all
   > \(a,b\in X\),
   > \[
   >  \delta_z(b)-\delta_z(a)\leq d(a,b)\leq \delta_z(b)+\delta_z(a),
   > \]
   > and
   > \[
   >  \delta_z(z)=0.
   > \]

items.title: Pointlike Functions with a Zero Are Point Functions
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(u:X\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\). Then
\(u\in\delta(X)\) if and only if \(u\) is pointlike on \(X\) and
\[
 0\in u(X).
\]
In that case, there is a unique \(w\in X\) such that \(u(w)=0\), and
\[
 u=\delta_w.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(u:X\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\). Then
   > \(u\in\delta(X)\) if and only if \(u\) is pointlike on \(X\) and
   > \[
   >  0\in u(X).
   > \]
   > In that case, there is a unique \(w\in X\) such that \(u(w)=0\), and
   > \[
   >  u=\delta_w.
   > \]

items.title: Open Balls are Open
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r>0\),
the open ball \(B_d(x;r)\) is open in \((X,d)\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r>0\),
   > the open ball \(B_d(x;r)\) is open in \((X,d)\).

items.title: Metric Open Set Closure Properties
Complement of a Closed Ball Is Open
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r\geq 0\),
\[
 X\setminus \overline{B}_d(x;r)
 =
 \{\,y\in X:d(x,y)>r\,\}
\]
is open.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r\geq 0\),
   > \[
   >  X\setminus \overline{B}_d(x;r)
   >  =
   >  \{\,y\in X:d(x,y)>r\,\}
   > \]
   > is open.

items.title: Closed Balls Are Closed
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r\geq 0\),
the closed ball
\[
 \overline{B}_d(x;r)=\{\,y\in X:d(x,y)\leq r\,\}
\]
is closed.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r\geq 0\),
   > the closed ball
   > \[
   >  \overline{B}_d(x;r)=\{\,y\in X:d(x,y)\leq r\,\}
   > \]
   > is closed.

items.title: Closure of an Open Ball Is Contained in the Closed Ball
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r>0\),
\[
 \operatorname{cl}\bigl(B_d(x;r)\bigr)\subseteq \overline{B}_d(x;r).
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. For every \(x\in X\) and every \(r>0\),
   > \[
   >  \operatorname{cl}\bigl(B_d(x;r)\bigr)\subseteq \overline{B}_d(x;r).
   > \]

items.title: Interior is the Largest Open Subset
Metric Neighborhood Criterion for Sequential Convergence
items.statement:
Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(\{x_n\}\) be a sequence in \(X\), and
let \(x\in X\). Then
\[
 x_n\to x
\]
if and only if every neighborhood of \(x\) contains all but finitely many terms
of \(\{x_n\}\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(\{x_n\}\) be a sequence in \(X\), and
   > let \(x\in X\). Then
   > \[
   >  x_n\to x
   > \]
   > if and only if every neighborhood of \(x\) contains all but finitely many terms
   > of \(\{x_n\}\).

items.title: Metric Convergent Sequences Have Unique Limits
items.statement: In metric spaces, convergent sequences have unique limits.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In metric spaces, convergent sequences have unique limits.

items.title: Metric Cauchy Sequence with Convergent Subsequence
items.statement:
Let \(\{x_n\}\) be a Cauchy sequence in a metric space \((X,d)\), let
\(x\in X\), and let \(\{x_{n_k}\}\) be a subsequence of \(\{x_n\}\) such that
\[
 \lim_{k\to\infty}x_{n_k}=x.
\]
Then \(x_n\to x\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(\{x_n\}\) be a Cauchy sequence in a metric space \((X,d)\), let
   > \(x\in X\), and let \(\{x_{n_k}\}\) be a subsequence of \(\{x_n\}\) such that
   > \[
   >  \lim_{k\to\infty}x_{n_k}=x.
   > \]
   > Then \(x_n\to x\).

items.title: Coordinatewise Sequences in \(\mathbb{R}^m\)
items.statement:
Let \(\{x_n\}\) be a sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and let
\(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Write
\[
 x_n=\bigl(x_n^{(1)},\ldots,x_n^{(m)}\bigr)
 \qquad\text{for all } n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}.
\]
Then:
- \(x_n\to x_0\) if and only if
 \(x_n^{(j)}\to x_0^{(j)}\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
- \(\{x_n\}\) is Cauchy if and only if
 \(\{x_n^{(j)}\}\) is Cauchy for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(\{x_n\}\) be a sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and let
   > \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Write
   > \[
   >  x_n=\bigl(x_n^{(1)},\ldots,x_n^{(m)}\bigr)
   >  \qquad\text{for all } n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}.
   > \]
   > Then:
   > - \(x_n\to x_0\) if and only if
   >  \(x_n^{(j)}\to x_0^{(j)}\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
   > - \(\{x_n\}\) is Cauchy if and only if
   >  \(\{x_n^{(j)}\}\) is Cauchy for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).

items.title: Euclidean Cauchy Sequences Converge
items.statement: Every Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is convergent in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is convergent in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).

items.title: Pointwise Characterization of a Basis
items.statement:
Let \((X,\tau)\) be a topological space, and let
\(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\tau\). Then \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis for \(\tau\)
if and only if for every open set \(O\in\tau\) and every \(x\in O\), there is
\(B\in\mathcal{B}\) such that
\[
 x\in B\subseteq O.
\]
Consequently, a subset \(A\subseteq X\) is open if and only if for each
\(x\in A\), there is \(B\in\mathcal{B}\) such that
\[
 x\in B\subseteq A.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \((X,\tau)\) be a topological space, and let
   > \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\tau\). Then \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis for \(\tau\)
   > if and only if for every open set \(O\in\tau\) and every \(x\in O\), there is
   > \(B\in\mathcal{B}\) such that
   > \[
   >  x\in B\subseteq O.
   > \]
   > Consequently, a subset \(A\subseteq X\) is open if and only if for each
   > \(x\in A\), there is \(B\in\mathcal{B}\) such that
   > \[
   >  x\in B\subseteq A.
   > \]

items.title: Closed-Set Characterization of Topologies
items.statement:
Let \(X\) be a set, and let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a collection of subsets of
\(X\). Suppose that:
- \(\emptyset\in\mathcal{C}\) and \(X\in\mathcal{C}\);
- the intersection of any family of elements of \(\mathcal{C}\) belongs
 to \(\mathcal{C}\);
- the union of any two elements of \(\mathcal{C}\) belongs to
 \(\mathcal{C}\).
Then there is a unique topology \(\tau\) on \(X\) whose family of closed sets
is exactly \(\mathcal{C}\).
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(X\) be a set, and let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a collection of subsets of
   > \(X\). Suppose that:
   > - \(\emptyset\in\mathcal{C}\) and \(X\in\mathcal{C}\);
   > - the intersection of any family of elements of \(\mathcal{C}\) belongs
   >  to \(\mathcal{C}\);
   > - the union of any two elements of \(\mathcal{C}\) belongs to
   >  \(\mathcal{C}\).
   > Then there is a unique topology \(\tau\) on \(X\) whose family of closed sets
   > is exactly \(\mathcal{C}\).

items.title: Intersection of $\sigma$-algebras is a $\sigma$-algebra
items.statement:
Let $\{\mathcal{M}_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}$ be any family of $\sigma$-algebras
on $X$ (indexed by any set $I$). Then
\[
\mathcal{M} \;:=\; \bigcap_{\alpha \in I} \mathcal{M}_\alpha
\]
is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\{\mathcal{M}_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}$ be any family of $\sigma$-algebras
   > on $X$ (indexed by any set $I$). Then
   > \[
   > \mathcal{M} \;:=\; \bigcap_{\alpha \in I} \mathcal{M}_\alpha
   > \]
   > is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$.

items.title: Identity Collapse and Uniqueness
items.statement:
If $\star$ has a left identity $e_L$ and a right identity $e_R$, then
$e_L=e_R$. Consequently a two-sided identity, if it exists, is unique.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\star$ has a left identity $e_L$ and a right identity $e_R$, then
   > $e_L=e_R$. Consequently a two-sided identity, if it exists, is unique.

items.title: Uniqueness of the Absorbing Element
items.statement: A two-sided absorbing element, if it exists, is unique.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A two-sided absorbing element, if it exists, is unique.

items.title: General Associativity
items.statement:
If $\star$ is associative, then any finite product
$a_1\star a_2\star\cdots\star a_n$ has a value independent of
parenthesization.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\star$ is associative, then any finite product
   > $a_1\star a_2\star\cdots\star a_n$ has a value independent of
   > parenthesization.

items.title: Inverse Collapse and Uniqueness in a Monoid
items.statement:
If $\star$ is associative with identity $e$, and $a$ has a left inverse $b$
and a right inverse $c$, then $b=c$. Hence the inverse of an invertible
element is unique.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $\star$ is associative with identity $e$, and $a$ has a left inverse $b$
   > and a right inverse $c$, then $b=c$. Hence the inverse of an invertible
   > element is unique.

items.title: Units of a Monoid Form a Group
items.statement:
In a monoid $(A,\star,e)$, the set $A^\times$ of invertible elements is
closed under $\star$ and forms a group.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a monoid $(A,\star,e)$, the set $A^\times$ of invertible elements is
   > closed under $\star$ and forms a group.

items.title: Invertible Implies Cancellable
items.statement: In a monoid, every invertible element is cancellable.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a monoid, every invertible element is cancellable.

items.title: Uniqueness of the Identity in a Group
items.statement: The identity of a group is unique.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The identity of a group is unique.

items.title: Uniqueness of Inverses in a Group
items.statement: Each element of a group has a unique inverse.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Each element of a group has a unique inverse.

items.title: Cancellation Laws in a Group
items.statement: In a group, $ab=ac$ implies $b=c$, and $ba=ca$ implies $b=c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a group, $ab=ac$ implies $b=c$, and $ba=ca$ implies $b=c$.

items.title: Socks--Shoes
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a group, $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}$.

items.title: Multiplication by Zero
items.statement: In a ring, $a\cdot 0=0\cdot a=0$ for all $a$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a ring, $a\cdot 0=0\cdot a=0$ for all $a$.

items.title: Multiplication by Additive Inverse
items.statement:
In a ring,
\[
a\cdot(-b)=-(a\cdot b)=(-a)\cdot b.
\]
In a ring, $(-1)\cdot a=-a$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In a ring,
   > \[
   > a\cdot(-b)=-(a\cdot b)=(-a)\cdot b.
   > \]
   > In a ring, $(-1)\cdot a=-a$.

items.title: Cancellation in Integral Domains
items.statement: In an integral domain, if $a\neq 0$ and $ab=ac$, then $b=c$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > In an integral domain, if $a\neq 0$ and $ab=ac$, then $b=c$.

items.title: Every Field is an Integral Domain
items.statement: Every field is an integral domain.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every field is an integral domain.

items.title: Finite Integral Domain is a Field
items.statement: Every finite integral domain is a field.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every finite integral domain is a field.

items.title: Hilbert Basis Theorem
items.statement:
If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, then the polynomial ring $R[x]$
is also Noetherian.

In particular, $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is Noetherian for any field $k$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, then the polynomial ring $R[x]$
   > is also Noetherian.
   >
   > In particular, $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is Noetherian for any field $k$.

items.title: Addition Is Commutative in $\mathbf{F}^n$
items.statement:
For all $x,y \in \mathbf{F}^n$,
\[
x+y=y+x.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For all $x,y \in \mathbf{F}^n$,
   > \[
   > x+y=y+x.
   > \]

items.title: Unique Additive Identity
items.statement: A vector space has a unique additive identity.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > A vector space has a unique additive identity.

items.title: Unique Additive Inverse
items.statement: Every vector in a vector space has a unique additive inverse.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Every vector in a vector space has a unique additive inverse.

items.title: $0v=0$
items.statement:
For every $v \in V$,
\[
0v=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $v \in V$,
   > \[
   > 0v=0.
   > \]

items.title: $a0=0$
items.statement:
For every $a \in \mathbf{F}$,
\[
a0=0.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $a \in \mathbf{F}$,
   > \[
   > a0=0.
   > \]

items.title: $(-1)v=-v$
items.statement:
For every $v \in V$,
\[
(-1)v=-v.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > For every $v \in V$,
   > \[
   > (-1)v=-v.
   > \]

items.title: Conditions for a Subspace
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbf{F}$ and let $U \subseteq V$.
   > Then $U$ is a subspace of $V$ if and only if the following three conditions hold:
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - $0 \in U$;
   > - for all $u,v \in U$, one has $u+v \in U$;
   > - for all $a \in \mathbf{F}$ and all $u \in U$, one has $au \in U$.

items.title: Sum of Subspaces Is the Smallest Containing Subspace
items.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbf{F}$, and let
$U_1,\dots,U_m$ be subspaces of $V$.
Then $U_1+\cdots+U_m$ is a subspace of $V$ containing each of
$U_1,\dots,U_m$.
Moreover, if $W$ is a subspace of $V$ containing each of
$U_1,\dots,U_m$, then
\[
U_1+\cdots+U_m \subseteq W.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbf{F}$, and let
   > $U_1,\dots,U_m$ be subspaces of $V$.
   > Then $U_1+\cdots+U_m$ is a subspace of $V$ containing each of
   > $U_1,\dots,U_m$.
   > Moreover, if $W$ is a subspace of $V$ containing each of
   > $U_1,\dots,U_m$, then
   > \[
   > U_1+\cdots+U_m \subseteq W.
   > \]

items.title: Condition for a Direct Sum
items.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbf{F}$, and let
$U_1,\dots,U_m$ be subspaces of $V$ such that
\[
V=U_1+\cdots+U_m.
\]
Then the following are equivalent:
- [label=(\roman*)]
- \(V=U_1\oplus\cdots\oplus U_m\);
- if \(u_1 \in U_1,\dots,u_m \in U_m\) and
 \[
 u_1+\cdots+u_m=0,
 \]
 then
 \[
 u_1=\cdots=u_m=0.
 \]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbf{F}$, and let
   > $U_1,\dots,U_m$ be subspaces of $V$ such that
   > \[
   > V=U_1+\cdots+U_m.
   > \]
   > Then the following are equivalent:
   > - [label=(\roman*)]
   > - \(V=U_1\oplus\cdots\oplus U_m\);
   > - if \(u_1 \in U_1,\dots,u_m \in U_m\) and
   >  \[
   >  u_1+\cdots+u_m=0,
   >  \]
   >  then
   >  \[
   >  u_1=\cdots=u_m=0.
   >  \]

items.title: Direct Sum of Two Subspaces
items.statement:
Let $U$ and $W$ be subspaces of a vector space $V$.
Then
\[
U+W=U\oplus W
\]
if and only if
\[
U \cap W = \{0\}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $U$ and $W$ be subspaces of a vector space $V$.
   > Then
   > \[
   > U+W=U\oplus W
   > \]
   > if and only if
   > \[
   > U \cap W = \{0\}.
   > \]

items.title: Characterizations of Order-Isomorphisms for Finite Posets
items.statement:
Let $(P, \leq_P)$ and $(Q, \leq_Q)$ be finite partially ordered sets and
let $\varphi : P \to Q$ be a bijection. The following are equivalent:
- $\varphi$ is an order-isomorphism.
- For all $x, y \in P$:\; $x <_P y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \varphi(x) <_Q \varphi(y)$.
- For all $x, y \in P$:\; $x \prec_P y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \varphi(x) \prec_Q \varphi(y)$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P, \leq_P)$ and $(Q, \leq_Q)$ be finite partially ordered sets and
   > let $\varphi : P \to Q$ be a bijection. The following are equivalent:
   > - $\varphi$ is an order-isomorphism.
   > - For all $x, y \in P$:\; $x <_P y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \varphi(x) <_Q \varphi(y)$.
   > - For all $x, y \in P$:\; $x \prec_P y \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \varphi(x) \prec_Q \varphi(y)$.

items.title: Hasse Diagram Characterization for Finite Posets
items.statement:
Let $(P, \leq_P)$ and $(Q, \leq_Q)$ be finite partially ordered sets.
Then $P$ and $Q$ are order-isomorphic if and only if their Hasse diagrams
are isomorphic as directed graphs --- that is, identical up to relabeling
of elements.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P, \leq_P)$ and $(Q, \leq_Q)$ be finite partially ordered sets.
   > Then $P$ and $Q$ are order-isomorphic if and only if their Hasse diagrams
   > are isomorphic as directed graphs --- that is, identical up to relabeling
   > of elements.

items.title: Duality Principle
items.statement:
Let $\Phi$ be a statement about partially ordered sets, expressed purely
in terms of $\leq$, that holds in every partially ordered set. Then the
dual statement $\Phi^{\mathrm{op}}$, obtained by replacing every
occurrence of $\leq$ with $\geq$, also holds in every partially ordered
set.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $\Phi$ be a statement about partially ordered sets, expressed purely
   > in terms of $\leq$, that holds in every partially ordered set. Then the
   > dual statement $\Phi^{\mathrm{op}}$, obtained by replacing every
   > occurrence of $\leq$ with $\geq$, also holds in every partially ordered
   > set.

items.title: Every Nonempty Finite Poset Has a Maximal Element
items.statement:
Let $(P, \leq)$ be a finite partially ordered set. Then every nonempty
subset $Q \subseteq P$ has at least one maximal element. Furthermore,
for every $x \in P$ there exists $y \in \operatorname{Max}(P)$ with
$x \leq y$.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P, \leq)$ be a finite partially ordered set. Then every nonempty
   > subset $Q \subseteq P$ has at least one maximal element. Furthermore,
   > for every $x \in P$ there exists $y \in \operatorname{Max}(P)$ with
   > $x \leq y$.

items.title: Predicates and Power Sets Are Order-Isomorphic
items.statement:
The map $\Phi : (\mathcal{P}^*(X), \leq) \to (\mathcal{P}(X), \subseteq)$
is an \hyperref[def:order-isomorphism]{order-isomorphism}.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > The map $\Phi : (\mathcal{P}^*(X), \leq) \to (\mathcal{P}(X), \subseteq)$
   > is an \hyperref[def:order-isomorphism]{order-isomorphism}.

items.title: Every Order-Embedding Is Injective
items.statement:
Let $(P, \leq_P)$ and $(Q, \leq_Q)$ be partially ordered sets, and let
$\varphi : P \to Q$ be an order-embedding. Then $\varphi$ is injective.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let $(P, \leq_P)$ and $(Q, \leq_Q)$ be partially ordered sets, and let
   > $\varphi : P \to Q$ be an order-embedding. Then $\varphi$ is injective.

items.title: Convex hull as the smallest convex set
items.statement:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\). Then \(\conv(P)\) is convex, contains \(P\), and
is contained in every convex set that contains \(P\). Hence
\[
 \conv(P)
 =
 \bigcap\{K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2 : K\text{ is convex and }P\subseteq K\}.
\]
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\). Then \(\conv(P)\) is convex, contains \(P\), and
   > is contained in every convex set that contains \(P\). Hence
   > \[
   >  \conv(P)
   >  =
   >  \bigcap\{K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2 : K\text{ is convex and }P\subseteq K\}.
   > \]

items.title: Supporting functional characterization of hull vertices
items.statement:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) be finite and in general position. A point \(p\in P\)
is a vertex of \(\conv(P)\) if and only if there exists a direction
\(d\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
 \langle d,p\rangle>\langle d,q\rangle
 \qquad
 \text{for all } q\in P\setminus\{p\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(p\) is the unique point of \(P\) attaining
\[
 \max_{q\in P}\langle d,q\rangle.
\]
Thus every hull vertex is a maximum of \(P\) under some linear functional.

items.title: Monotone slope characterization of the upper hull
items.statement:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) be finite and in general position. Let
\[
 v_0,v_1,\dots,v_m
\]
be the vertices of the upper hull of \(P\), listed in increasing
\(x\)-coordinate, and define
\[
 s_k
 =
 \frac{y(v_{k+1})-y(v_k)}{x(v_{k+1})-x(v_k)},
 \qquad
 k=0,1,\dots,m-1.
\]
Then
\[
 s_0>s_1>\cdots>s_{m-1}.
\]
Conversely, if points \(w_0,\dots,w_m\) satisfy
\[
 x(w_0)<x(w_1)<\cdots<x(w_m)
\]
and their consecutive slopes are strictly decreasing, then every \(w_k\) is a
vertex of
\[
 \conv(\{w_0,\dots,w_m\}).
\]
The lower hull is characterized similarly, with strictly increasing consecutive
slopes.
items.markdown:
> **Statement.**
   > Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) be finite and in general position. Let
   > \[
   >  v_0,v_1,\dots,v_m
   > \]
   > be the vertices of the upper hull of \(P\), listed in increasing
   > \(x\)-coordinate, and define
   > \[
   >  s_k
   >  =
   >  \frac{y(v_{k+1})-y(v_k)}{x(v_{k+1})-x(v_k)},

   > \]

   > \]
   > Conversely, if points \(w_0,\dots,w_m\) satisfy
   > \[
   >  x(w_0)<x(w_1)<\cdots<x(w_m)
   > \]
   > and their consecutive slopes are strictly decreasing, then every \(w_k\) is a
   > vertex of
   > \[
   >  \conv(\{w_0,\dots,w_m\}).
   > \]
   > The lower hull is characterized similarly, with strictly increasing consecutive
   > slopes.

items.title: Greedy slope construction of the upper hull
items.statement:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) be finite and in general position. Define
\[
 v_0=\argmin_{p\in P}x(p).
\]
Given \(v_k\) with
\[
 x(v_k)<\max_{p\in P}x(p),
\]
define
\[
 v_{k+1}
 =
 \argmax_{\substack{q\in P\\x(q)>x(v_k)}}
 \frac{y(q)-y(v_k)}{x(q)-x(v_k)}.
\]
Terminate once
\[
 v_k=\argmax_{p\in P}x(p).
\]
Then the points
\[
 v_0,v_1,\dots,v_m
\]
produced by this construction are exactly the vertices of the upper hull of
\(P\), and the slopes encountered along the way are strictly decreasing.
